As he so rightly said, there was a lot of collaboration in the House of Lords as our colleagues were taking through this Bill, and I certainly intend to enter the conversation in a similar spirit of collaboration over the coming weeks and months. As the Chancellor has said, the financial services sector is incredibly important to this country. It is the engine room that powers our economy. As the Chancellor has also said, it generates 8% of our national economic output, contributes £12 in every £100 of tax paid and makes up 3% of all jobs in the UK. As the Chancellor so rightly said, two thirds of those jobs are outside London. The sector truly is a jewel in our economic crown, but it is important to remember that financial services underpin our everyday lives—for example, they support my constituents in opening and running businesses. They support all our constituents across this great country to get on to the housing ladder. They support people across the UK in ways that are not truly understood, including financial support for their employer; ensuring that their homes and other assets are insured; providing liquidity to buy expensive items such as a car; and helping to provide for our retirement. What happens just a mile or so up the road and across the country helps every one of us in pretty much every aspect of our lives. Despite that, we must be careful. The UK’s financial services and related professional services sector are at a crossroads. TheCityUK published earlier this year its “No Time to Lose” report in conjunction with PwC, which I will quote directly. It said that “the hard truth is that overall industry growth has stalled over the last decade and the UK is falling behind other financial centres.” Our international competitiveness should be our priority, because the UK market is so internationally focused. As we know, London is the second-biggest financial services centre on the planet, second only to New York. However, while New York’s financial services market is 80% led by its domestic economy, here in the UK London is 80% international. At the most basic level, our international competitiveness is four times as valuable to us here as it is to the Americans across the Atlantic. The Chancellor rightly mentioned the Budget, during which he said to the banks that “I celebrate, and am grateful for, the role that you play.” —[ Official Report , 28 October 2026; Vol. 792, c. 307] , But then he increased the bank levy by 3%. To be fair to him, bank stocks did go up on the day, because they were expecting a 5% permanent levy. None the less, we have to bear in mind that that takes the marginal tax rate on banks to 49.5%. That is not competitive on the international stage. We need to be mindful of that, because we need to attract international banks to come to our shores, and it is very important that we get this right. We understand that that generates a little more tax, but we want more people to invest in this country, and that is why we were against that measure. It sends the wrong signal.

Will the hon. Member join me in congratulating J.P. Morgan? It is in its 40th year of operation in Bournemouth, and this year it is investing £350 million into Bournemouth and the wider UK economy. It is doing that because it sees the overriding talent in Bournemouth and across the UK. The Bournemouth site is the second-most important site across 38 in Europe, the middle east and Africa for the world’s largest bank and seventh-largest technologist. Is that not a vote of confidence in the UK economy?

The hon. Gentleman is absolutely right. It is incredibly important to remember that banks such as J.P. Morgan invest in the wider community, but Jamie Dimon has said that he is worried about uncertainty around the tax regime on banks in the UK. He has warned that if we are uncertain and increase the level of tax on banks, they will not invest another £300 million or so into Canary Wharf. That is the point: we have to be mindful of international competitiveness. It does not take much, when we are taxing close to 50% on banks, for them to change their mind and go to another financial services centre. However, the hon. Gentleman’s point is absolutely right: the value of international investment by banks in communities such as his is really important.

Following that last intervention on the tremendous importance of banks to this country, does my hon. Friend share my concern? Notwithstanding what it says on the face of the Finance Bill, I rather fear that a Labour Chancellor with this particular set of Back Benchers will not turn up after 15 months and say, “I have a great idea, comrades: let us get rid of the doubling of the bank tax.” I fear that there will be some other new financial pressure—there are always financial pressures—that will mean that this socialist Government further reduce the credit available to this country and make us all poorer as a result of satisfying Government Back Benchers, who understand nothing about economics.

My right hon. Friend makes a very reasonable point. It is certainly easier to tax banks than it is to cut benefits, for example, but we have to be careful about this. He raises a very good point; if we reduce the amount of cash available to banks, we reduce the amount of money getting into the wider economy. I will come to that a bit later in my speech. We have identified certain areas where we can make it easier for banks to lend more money in the economy, but, as I say, I will come to that in a minute. This Bill is an important opportunity to change the signal that we are sending to the wider world. We believe that, in general terms, this Bill takes steps in the right direction, so the Chancellor and the Economic Secretary to the Treasury will be glad to hear that we will not vote against it tonight. There is a one-line Whip, and it is fantastic that so many people have turned up on the Government Benches for this debate. However, while the Bill takes a positive step, it should be taking a positive leap. Just like the Budget, it feels like a missed opportunity to take the bold action needed. As I have said, we intend to work constructively with the Government, but we want them to be braver and go further. Let me be clear: when it comes to this Bill, we should be talking about the level of risk that we are willing to accept, not how we can pursue perfection. This is about how we can keep talent in the UK, not about how we can make it jump through more hoops. This is about how we can empower the financial services sector, not about how we can bind it in further red tape. This is about the bold action that we should take to cement the future of the sector, not about how we can tinker at the edges. I hope that colleagues will follow that advice as the Bill progresses. First, though, we should celebrate our past, because we have so much to be proud of in this country. The financial services ecosystem started in the UK in the 12th century, when the Knights Templar first issued receipts to pilgrims and crusaders for valuable assets such as gold. Those could be exchanged in the Holy Land for funds, creating what we recognise as the first iteration of bank notes. In the 17th century, Jonathan’s Coffee House was the first to advertise share prices. From there, the London stock exchange grew, setting up the model for equity ownership the world over. Similarly, Lloyd’s Coffee House created the insurance market that we see today. From that, the UK has continued to be a world leader in innovation, and we have built a reputation as a major financial centre. The statistics do not lie. We are the largest net exporter of financial services in the world, at £119 billion last year. The London market alone is larger than its five closest international competitors combined. We have the most unicorns in Europe, the second largest asset management sector globally, the third largest insurance market globally and the fifth largest domestic banking sector globally. The point is that we start in a good position, and we have a great deal to be proud of. However, if we are to continue to succeed today and in the future, we must be bold, and we must be aware that others seek to steal our advantage. We must respond to that challenge and restore our economic powerhouse. Where do we want the Government to go further? The first area is ringfencing. As the Chancellor alluded to earlier, the Bill talks about ringfencing, which, as we know, is the structural separation of certain retail banking activities from the activities conducted by international wholesale and investment banks. It was proposed by the Parliamentary Commission on Banking Standards back in 2013—following the Wright review, if I remember rightly—which was created in response to the global financial crisis. Let me be clear that ringfencing was well intentioned— I know that well, because I sat on the Parliamentary Commission on Banking Standards and was part of the process that recommended it. Ho

I am interested in the hon. Gentleman’s thoughtful comments and the research he is quoting, but he is now talking about removing ringfencing completely. Can he explain to the House how that would mitigate the risk posed by the bad players who led to some of the problems in 2008? As a result, some of us were in this place voting to nationalise banks, at a cost to the British taxpayer. How can the hon. Gentleman be confident that that could never happen again? We do not legislate for today; we legislate for the worst possible scenario—the mad, the bad and the dangerous—not the good people who I am sure he is talking about.

The point of ringfencing at the time was to separate the retail banks from the wholesale and investment banks. If the hon. Lady remembers, the Liikanen reforms sought to cage the tigers and ringfence the investment banks into units, whereas our reforms looked to put a fence around the deer park to look after the retail banks. The problem is that this creates a cliff edge as customers get past a certain turnover—I think they go from being in the retail bank to being in the wholesale bank when they get to £5 million of turnover. The only bank that has changed that is Barclays; it has set that limit at £100 million, which makes the retail bank much more open, and arguably could make it slightly more vulnerable. Of course we do not want the big banks to fail—although, having said that, we have to have an element of risk within the banking system. It is important that we keep that. However, we have a number of systems that have come in later and that other countries have looked at, such as the bail-in bonds and the MREL regime. Returning to the competitiveness point, we now find ourselves with a ringfencing regime that creates extra costs and administrative burdens for banks that other countries do not have. We also have a system that can protect consumers, the bail-in bonds, whereby we have regulatory capital that can potentially be converted from bonds into equity to solve that problem.

I am sure that many Members of this House would entertain the idea of taking a targeted look at the way in which ringfencing regulation is implemented and agree that, where it is helpful, there should be much more of a free flow of information and discussions with clients across universal banks. However, can the hon. Gentleman categorically rule out the complete abolition of ringfencing that he has suggested, if only for the sake of consumers who do not want to see their retail money swirling around in an investment bank?

The hon. Gentleman raises a number of points. We are getting deep into the debate, but the very quick answer to his question is no, I cannot rule out getting rid of the ringfencing regime. It has already been made public that the policy of a future Conservative Government will be to do so. That is the debate we will be having in Committee, and I am sure the hon. Gentleman will be delighted to join us in Committee, where we can get into the debate in depth. It is great to see so many Members across the House putting themselves forward with their enthusiasm to get involved in the debate—my right hon. Friend the Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) will have found a friend. My second point—of a number of points, although I am conscious that I am taking up a lot of time—is that we would like the Government to go further on bank capital requirements. UK banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms are required to maintain minimum levels of capital in proportion to their risk-weighted assets. That is to help ensure that firms remain resilient and to reduce the impact of failure. Clearly, no responsible Government would abolish capital requirements, but we need to question whether banks should be required to hold capital beyond what is genuinely needed for resilience. This is an important point. We should acknowledge that the Bank of England has eased bank capital requirements in recent years, specifically at the end of 2025, when it revised down the benchmark for tier 1 capital from 14% of risk-weighted assets to 13%. However, it is worth remembering that the Parliamentary Commission on Banking Standards recommended 11%, so that benchmark is higher than we originally asked for. We believe that the current level is still too high. The most recent stress test carried out by the Bank of England found that “all banks remained above their set capital minima at the low-point of the scenario. No individual bank was required to strengthen its capital position as a result of the test.” From memory, it was a one-in-250-year event that the banks were being stress tested on. The system has to allow an element of risk—when I was on the banking commission, we made it very clear how important that was. We made it clear that it was okay for a bank to fail, but it was not okay for banks to bring down the entire system. The important point is that there has to be an element of risk in the system, but that is not what has been delivered, meaning that the potential lending and financing capacity of our banking sector is significantly reduced—to the tune of about £450 billion each year, we reckon. That is an awful lot of money that is not going into the economy. UK Finance has advised me that each percentage point of the tier 1 capital stack potentially represents about £600 billion in liquidity, so 2% above the recommendation of the Parliamentary Commission on Banking Standards represents about £1.2 trillion. Leverage that up under the banks and we are potentially talking about £12 trillion that is not in circulation because of over-interpretation of the rules. But we do not want to get ahead of ourselves; we reckon that £450 billion is not in circulation because of that over-enthusiasm on the tier 1 stack. That is money that could be used more productively. It could be invested in our communities or in businesses, but it remains stuck on banks’ balance sheets. While the Bill does not contain any specific measures dealing with bank capital requirements, we believe that it is a perfect opportunity to make the necessary changes—specifically, to reform the parameters within which the Financial Policy Committee and the PRA operate. As such, we will be putting forward changes in areas where we believe the Government may be encouraged to take some advice from the Opposition. As we have heard, the Financial Ombudsman Service plays an incredibly important role in the UK financial services sector. It provides redress for consumers

We are getting there. As I said at the beginning of my speech, the UK is a major financial centre with a rich history of innovation. We cannot afford to lose that reputation, so we must also be looking to the future. Digital assets will be a key part of that, as will the technologies that underpin them. We have been told time and again that the UK has no clear direction on digital assets, meaning that companies in the UK are being restricted from innovating, so we need to create a strategy that sends a clear signal to that industry. That is why the digital assets strategy in clause 50, which was introduced in the other place, is so important. We tabled that amendment in the Lords for a few reasons. First, we want to send a clear message about where the UK is going; it is incredibly important that we define what the UK’s ambition is. Secondly, going back to the competitiveness point, other jurisdictions have these strategies. Thirdly, the significance of digital assets has not been identified in any recent Government strategy. Finally, the digital assets sector is incredibly diverse, beyond where the Government are currently looking—it is very innovative. For all of those reasons, we believe that the digital assets strategy and clause 50 are necessary, and that removing that clause from the Bill—if that is the Government intend to do—would send the wrong message to the sector. Do not take our word for it; take the word of the organisations that support clause 50: the UK Cryptoasset Business Council, TheCityUK, Innovate Finance, the Payments Association, techUK, Global Digital Finance, the Crypto Council for Innovation, the International Digital Assets Counsel Association, CryptoUK and the Digital Money Association. All of those organisations know that “Other jurisdictions are moving rapidly to attract digital-asset businesses, investment and talent.” A clear strategy will help the UK to keep up with those other jurisdictions and demonstrate that we are embracing these new technologies. I know that the Economic Secretary to the Treasury feels passionately about this area of her brief, so I hope she will use her closing remarks—we will all be waiting in the Chamber until 10 o’clock to hear them—to reassure the industry and commit to retaining the digital assets strategy in the Bill. To conclude, financial services and the related professional services are incredibly important to the UK. When they succeed, they help to empower our communities and unlock growth. The Economic Secretary to the Treasury understands that. She has a very good reputation in the City of London as being somebody who gets it, so I look forward to working with her over the next few weeks and months. I am sure we will have our disagreements, but where we do, it will be about the detail, not the overall direction of this Bill. I know we can remain focused on empowering the sector. The financial services sector is also important to me personally. I spent the bulk of my working life—27 years—working in the City, and I know the amazing things it can do. Being the shadow Economic Secretary to the Treasury, I have seen at first hand that we still have so much potential across this great country of ours. If we get this Bill right, we can unlock even more. While the financial services sector may be at a crossroads, it is now time for us to get behind the sector, to shift into gear, to accelerate our efforts and to focus on the exciting journey ahead.

I agree with both the Chancellor and the shadow Economic Secretary, the hon. Member for Wyre Forest (Mark Garnier) that the financial services sector has an important part to play in our economy. As the shadow Economic Secretary said, the sector represents 3% of jobs in the UK, and it is important for growth and investment. It is therefore important that we understand its role and that we get things right. This Bill, in the Government’s terms, “will modernise how the sector is regulated, and enable it to grow and lend more to businesses. It will also make consumer protections fit for the digital age”. I do not think any of us would disagree with those intentions. The Government have also set out clearly that they want to maintain high standards of regulation and oversight at the same time. There is a balance to be struck in leaning in to support a sector, while also protecting the many consumers—millions of our constituents—who are borrowing, investing and using the services of financial institutions. Having a strong and competitive financial services sector is important for driving growth, but the protection of consumers is important, too. The Treasury Committee has looked at that balance between the growth objective that the previous Chancellor set the Financial Conduct Authority and its role in regulation. As a side point, I mention remit letters. The new Chancellor has not had a chance to write too many yet, but the number of remit letters that go to our regulators runs into quite high numbers. Those bodies then have to consider the “have regard to” comments in those letters in their work, and it makes for a very long list of things to do, some of which just cannot all be done at the same time. The Treasury could look to prune some of these requirements, or to decide what the key areas are at any point, so that those organisations know what they should be focusing on. This Bill could be seen as moving the pendulum more towards the financial services sector and further from regulation to support consumers, and we should be careful about that. The Committee has made some comments on it, but for me, consumers should be front and centre. My question to the Government—the Economic Secretary may expand on this in her closing remarks—is: how far should that pendulum swing? How far is too far? Who is the arbiter of what level of protection constituents and consumers should expect? We have a number of bodies, and I will speak about the Financial Ombudsman Service a little later. It is not just me or the Treasury Committee who have been raising these issues. Nikhil Rathi, the chief executive of the Financial Conduct Authority, said to us in July that the FCA needs a clear indication of the Government’s risk tolerance when it comes to markets. He is up for the challenge, but he needs to know as a regulator where to draw the line between promoting growth and consumer protection. We know that even a small increase in the percentage of customers harmed is a lot of people. One of the pleasures of our role as MPs is that we get to see people face to face at our surgeries. We see people in the raw. Whitehall is a long way from that direct contact, and it is us who will be picking up the problems if they arise. As this Bill proceeds through Committee, we need to be cautious and make sure that we are stress-testing that point about consumer protection at each stage. The Government are encouraging more investment. In fact, the Economic Secretary, during her previous time as Economic Secretary, made a number of public statements encouraging people to invest more. I can understand the Government’s position. People can make a lot more money from savings if they invest them carefully and well, but it is about changing the language. There has been concern about investment, particularly since the financial crash of 2008—it is a bit like the “Smoking kills” signs on cigarette packets—so the Government are changing the language, but I need to ask wha
Does my hon. Friend, who chairs the Treasury Committee, agree that in other jurisdictions it is quite common to have more parliamentary oversight of these sorts of appointments?

I agree with my hon. Friend, who is also a member of the Treasury Committee and a constituency neighbour of mine in London. We are not suggesting for a moment that the Treasury Committee starts rolling up its sleeves, conducting job interviews or getting in CVs. That is not our role. Our role is to be a check and a balance on the Government. As I said to the Opposition Front Bench spokesman, the hon. Member for Wyre Forest, we are not legislating for the people here in this Chamber, who I believe are good and honourable Members with all good intent. We have to legislate for the worst possible set of legislators and the worst possible Government, and we need to make sure that we have that commitment to the independence of the Financial Ombudsman Service. This would be one small step that would take nothing away from the rest of the Bill. It would not damage any of the Government’s set-out intentions. I know that the Chancellor is a strong advocate for a strong Parliament, and he should be praised and recognised for that, so I hope he will consider this option. I am happy to share my thoughts with the Economic Secretary on how an amendment could be tabled; it may be that it can come up in Committee—I would hope that it would not have to wait until a later stage, on Report. It is essential that the Chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service, which is a key public role, has the necessary independence and professional skills to maintain the balance between consumers and the financial services industry. The Treasury Committee has a number of pre-appointment hearings—more than a number of Committees do—and our measure is professional competence and independence. I would hope—and so far, Members will be glad to know, this has proved to be the case—that when the Treasury goes through a proper recruitment process, it recruits people with professional competence. We measure against that. Again, if there were a mad, bad or dangerous Government in future, that might not always be the case, but so far it has been. The independence point is important too, and that is what is often tested in the room when we have someone before us for a pre-appointment hearing. We do not have a power to sack, but in this case, we think we should have an extra power of a lock on that appointment. The Financial Ombudsman Service is accountable to Parliament. The Treasury Committee was compelled, due to the actions of a previous chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service, to underline that point in our ninth report of the session 2024-25, which was entitled— I say this for Hansard ’s purposes and I am sure that colleagues will avidly look this up in a moment—“Financial Ombudsman Service: Accountability to the House of Commons”. Providing the Treasury Committee with a statutory lock on the appointment of the FOS chair would help to guard against a repeat of that incident. I was saddened at the time to receive a letter from a public appointee to say that they did not have to appear in front of the Treasury Committee because they were a Member of the other place. That is another issue that I will take up in due course. The Second Reading debate is obviously about arguments in principle, but I am happy to have a further conversation with the Economic Secretary on the detail. I want to raise a couple of other quick points while I have the floor. On financial inclusion, I know the Economic Secretary has played her part—I think four Economic Secretaries have dealt with the financial inclusion strategy. Now that it has been published, the Committee will keep an eye on how it is going. We published a report on the matter, and the Government told the Committee that the Bill would include a reserve power on access to face-to-face banking services, recognising the limitations of voluntary action. The power was removed in the other place following concerns about its breadth. In their response to our report, the Government said they intended to restore that power during the passa

I entirely agree with the point my hon. Friend is making. In my constituency of Ealing Southall, Santander and NatWest have recently closed down, although Barclays is still there and is being refurbished. There is a very large north Indian population in the constituency and many of them are first generation, with English as another language. Does my hon. Friend agree that face-to-face banking is particularly important for those people and for older communities?

My hon. Friend raises an important point, because there are many excluded groups. There is an important challenge here, too. I am proud to be the Member of Parliament for Hackney South and Shoreditch, representing a very high percentage of fintech companies. Of course, those companies never had branches on the street, so it is not unreasonable for the larger banks, which have had a network of high street banks, to say that the playing field is not level. Some tech innovation has been amazing, making banking very accessible to some people, but there are still points in life—for instance, death, or maturity to 18 when products have to be turned from junior to adult—when we need to have conversations face to face. Even if it is not very often, there will be times when even the most digitally-savvy will need to have face-to-face contact. I recognise this is a difficult challenge for the Government to wrestle with, and there is no easy, simple answer, but it is important if there is to be financial inclusion. The danger is that if there is no proper ability to have contact with trusted banks, people get advice from elsewhere—a friend or a relative—that is not good advice; I have seen that in my own constituency. There is a danger that people get driven to the wrong place if we do not have a lock on some sort of provision, though I recognise that particular challenge for the Government.

One of the encouraging things in the financial inclusion strategy was a proposal to build a coalition of employers willing to offer a payroll deduction service to their employees to join and save with a credit union. Does my hon. Friend think that one of the ways to give that coalition new life and new energy would be if more parts of Whitehall—perhaps even the Treasury itself—were willing to make that commitment?

There we go: a stretch target for the Chancellor to sign up every civil servant in his Department to a credit union. I am sure that he is listening closely to that suggestion. I do not want to segue too much from the subject, but many years ago I tried to establish a mutual in Government and there was a limited understanding of what that meant. I am proud that we now have a co-operatives champion in my hon. Friend the Member for Peterborough (Andrew Pakes)—a Labour and Co-operative MP—who has access to all areas and can go in and challenge, shake up and educate parts of Whitehall about the benefits of mutuals. To finish on financial inclusion, the financial inclusion strategy is a good first step, but we said that the Government cannot rely solely on voluntary action from financial services to drive financial inclusion. We have made our comments clear in our report, and I hope that we will continue that dialogue with the Government to ensure that financial inclusion is a real thing. There has been some talk about access to capital markets in the banking sector, but there is a particular issue for building societies too. It is interesting how very few failures and repossessions there are with some building societies. I was talking recently to the chief executive of Skipton Building Society, whose default rate is very low—in fact, a number of those are people who have voluntarily given up their mortgage. That means the building society’s repossession rate is even lower, yet it has to capitalise to a very high degree to ensure that it is covering any potential losses. I think there is a real opportunity there. As was raised earlier, changes to credit unions are necessary and overdue. We have seen some of the measures for co-ops and mutuals in government get stuck, whether with the Law Commission or somewhere in the depths of Whitehall. We now have an agenda in government to double the size of the co-operative sector. We are seeing a strong building society sector and a mutual sector in finance. We have an opportunity to get credit unions on a stable footing. This is the opportunity to ensure that we get those things in place so that they are embedded and we make sure that the sector works and delivers. If it is about growth in every postcode, those are the organisations that reach every postcode, that are from the grassroots up and that can make this Financial Services and Markets Bill much more relevant to the people on the ground. It is not that the City of London is not relevant to me in my constituency and to a number of us who neighbour it, but for people in other parts of the country, Whitehall and the City seem like a long way away. Having co-ops and mutuals written in is important. I hope that the Economic Secretary will respond to some of those points when she sums up.

The UK financial services industry is vital to our economy. It enables us all to buy houses and cars, to save and invest safely and to insure against bad outcomes; it provides millions of jobs, not only in London but right across the UK; and it contributes hundreds of billions of pounds to GDP. It is one of the UK’s only world-leading industries. We have 160 foreign banks in the City and twice as many US dollars are traded on the UK foreign exchange in the UK than in the US. We have the largest source of pension funds in Europe—and if I mention Europe, as a Liberal Democrat I must also mention Brexit. It is true that the UK financial services industry has remained strong after Brexit. Of course it has: it is a world-leading industry that has many advantages beyond its access to European markets. We have, for instance, the advantages of location, language and law, and there is enormous talent here in the capital. However, we should not mistake that resilience for evidence that Brexit did not harm financial services. Exports of financial services have declined by 5.9%, and, according to TheCityUK, that is at least partly due to Brexit frictions. The loss of passporting rights, for example, makes it harder to acquire clients across the continent. Compliance and administrative costs have risen, and we are now less attractive in relation to becoming a pan-European headquarters. Whatever the dispute may be when it comes to the precise numerical impact of Brexit on financial services, this negative track has to be acknowledged.

I recognise the case that the hon. Gentleman is quite predictably making on Brexit, but given that we are where we are, what does he think would be the view of the financial services sector and the City of London on changes to where we are now?

Uncertainty is always unwelcome in the financial services industry, but Governments must make decisions for the very long run, and I think that in the very long run it would be in our best interests to be part of the single market again. The industry has remained resilient, not only in the face of Brexit but in the face of other challenges, but that should not be taken for granted. It is due, at least in part, to hard work and the reforms that were introduced after the 2008 financial crash. Prior to that, a reckless, deregulatory and ignorantly optimistic environment led to a complete and utter disaster, and not only for the industry but for society as a whole. The debts that stacked up in response to that crash are still squeezing the present Government’s potential to deliver better public services or lower taxes to this day, and the reputation of the industry among the public still suffers because of that event. However, it is worth stressing that the reforms made in the aftermath have broadly worked. The sector has remained financially stable. Repossessions are low, pension funds are healthy and stable, and bank failure is rarely speculated about—and if it were to happen, I trust that it would happen in an orderly way. This has remained the case despite some serious stress tests in recent years, not least the global pandemic and the global energy shocks, and it shows that measures such as the bank capital requirements, the liquidity rules and the ringfencing have created a system that can hold. I think that the Government should be mindful of that as they set out on a path to—in their own words—deregulate again. They should resist the Conservative party’s calls to abolish ringfencing entirely. I think that savers across the country will be shocked to hear that there is a party advocating for that money once again to become available to the investment banking industry. In a wider context, the Government should tread cautiously. They should not fall for the same old cycle of deregulation, crisis, and then regulation again. Instead, they should try to plot a more stable path through this moment. Nevertheless, there of course remains a case for reform. We are decades on from the financial crisis, and there will be plenty to do to modernise, to move with the times, to learn lessons, to tidy, to simplify, to clarify and to adjust, to make our financial services system work for the 21st-century economy. There is much to be supported in the Bill. I support, for instance, the move to make the Payment Systems Regulator part of the Financial Conduct Authority, and I hope that will mean we can continue some of the good work on open finance. I broadly support what I think is the intention in relation to improvements in access to banking, although we have yet to see some of the detail because we are waiting for the review to be published. I support the move to expand credit unions, and of course I support the intention to table amendments on child trust funds, for which I credit my hon. Friend the Member for Horsham (John Milne) and my right hon. Friend the Member for Kingston and Surbiton (Ed Davey). More broadly, the Liberal Democrats support the thrust of the Bill, but there are some key areas where we want to work with the Government to get this rare opportunity for reform right. In particular, on consumer protection I fear that the Bill is in danger of overcorrecting. It starts from a false premise, which is that consumer rights and economic growth are somehow in contention. They are not; they are two sides of the same coin. There can be no booming economy without consumer confidence, and poorer protection and more difficult redress are in the interests of neither consumers nor firms. I am struck by the volume of lobbying material that I receive from industry, and by how little I receive from the voice of the consumer. It is because of that inequality of arms that we in this place should be so mindful of the decisions we make in res

I, too, welcome this legislation and its goal of modernising consumer protection arrangements and making them fit for the digital age. I congratulate the Chancellor and the Economic Secretary to the Treasury on their work, and on their ongoing engagement with Members from across the House as the reforms proceed. I am very pleased to see measures that enable credit unions to expand by widening access to membership. I have seen the challenges experienced over the years as a Labour and Co-op MP, and I have worked to increase access to credit unions for local people in Feltham and Heston. It has been a challenge, and I look forward to working with my hon. Friend the Member for Peterborough (Andrew Pakes) on these reforms and on making sure that they become a reality for our constituents. It is clear that if anything can focus our mind’s eye on how important this is, it is seeing the importance of household resilience and being able to plan financially, given the challenges that the cost of living crisis has brought. It is important for us to think ahead and make sure that we do all we can to improve household resilience, and these reforms will help more than 200 credit unions across Great Britain to reach new communities, with millions of people having more access to affordable and community-based financial services. Credit unions are known and trusted by local communities, and trust is really important for giving people confidence about where to save, how to save and whom to trust. It is also vital that we take steps to protect access to in-person banking services for the future, and we look forward with anticipation to the publication of the access to banking review and the Government’s response. I want to raise three matters that I believe need to be further addressed in the Bill, some of which have already been referred to: the proposed 10-year time limit on complaints, the referrals process, and the fair and reasonable test. Finally, I will mention mortgage prisoners, as discussed by the Liberal Democrats’ spokesperson, the hon. Member for Carshalton and Wallington (Bobby Dean) First, on the 10-year time limit, the Government are putting forward a wide range of reforms to the Financial Ombudsman Service, but I am concerned that they are not being clear about the impacts on the public. The proposed 10-year time limit on Financial Ombudsman Service complaints risks locking thousands of consumers out of compensation. It can take years for people to realise that they have been ripped off, and firms often do everything they can to conceal misconduct.

On that point, one of the issues is document retention. Firms do not necessarily keep information, so the process can rely on the consumer keeping it. Even if they can get redress from a firm, they may not have the documentation.

I think we all agree with my hon. Friend’s important point. I am concerned that the Government’s assessment appears to underestimate the true cost by assuming that historical cases are worth little more than average complaints, and by ignoring many complaints that firms will simply reject, without considering their merits, due to the application of the new time limit. I am very happy to share with the Minister more of my analysis of the implications and of what is in the impact assessment. Secondly, the process of referral to the FCA could create a bureaucratic logjam, with firms incentivised to seek FCA rulings whenever a case looks likely to go against them, adding delay and administrative costs while allowing binding interpretations of the rules to be made without proper consultation. The referrals process should be reformed so that it is a rare occurrence, rather than the 1,000 to 3,000 referrals a year that the FCA expects will happen, which will cause delays as well as administrative costs and all the pain that that will entail. Proper consultation needs to be built in, so that the FCA gets full input from consumer groups before making binding decisions on what the new rules mean. Thirdly, there are important questions about changes to the ombudsman’s fair and reasonable test, which could narrow the ability of the FOS to take account of industry codes and good practice, including protections that victims of economic and financial abuse rely on. If we want economic growth, we need consumers to save for retirement, take out insurance and engage confidently with long-term financial products. We need small businesses, like many of those across Feltham and Heston, to borrow and invest, and undermining trust in dispute resolution mechanisms risks undermining that confidence. Martin Lewis has warned that “Restricting consumers’ access to free and fair redress is not a recipe for economic growth. Once consumers are warned about the erosion of their rights, it’s possible it will lead to disengagement from the financial services industry and diminishing trust.” That is why we must look very closely at the proposals in order that we are confident that consumers will retain the necessary confidence in financial services. Finally, in the last Parliament, the all-party parliamentary group on mortgage prisoners, which I co-chaired for a number of years following the experience of mortgage prisoners in Feltham and Heston, raised concerns that poor decision making at the FOS was leading to detriment for mortgage prisoners. In all honesty, no real progress was made. The situation is ongoing, as thousands of mortgage prisoners remain stuck and are suffering significant detriment. Many are still trapped on expensive variable rates with inactive lenders and are unable to switch to cheaper deals, so they are paying hundreds or thousands of pounds more each year and facing a far greater risk of losing their homes. In 2024, the previous Prime Minister promised to get everyone around the table and ensure that this issue was properly addressed, but that has not yet happened. Mortgage prisoners remain trapped, and are paying higher interest rates to inactive lenders and vulture funds. They are told that they cannot pass affordability tests in order to pay less for their mortgage, and as the Bank of England increases interest rates following six cuts, there is nothing that vulnerable mortgage prisoners can do to gain any certainty on their payments. Many are former Northern Rock customers who are still experiencing severe harm because their loans were sold to inactive lenders by the previous Conservative Government. The London School of Economics report, funded by Martin Lewis, put forward solutions including improved access to financial advice, targeted equity loan schemes, and a Government-backed guarantee mechanism to help borrowers move back into the active market. I would be grateful to hear when the Government plan to respond in full to the p
Order. After John Glen, I will introduce an immediate eight-minute time limit.

I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, and to my ministerial experience as the Economic Secretary between January 2018 and July 2022. Listening to the opening speeches gave me pause to reflect on some of my decisions. I hope that I am the sort of politician who is ready to concede where I did not go far enough or where mistakes were made, but after I have gone through some of the measures in this Bill, I want to offer some broader observations about the interaction between the Treasury, this place and our regulators, because it goes to the heart of how we move forward effectively as a country. as the shadow Economic Secretary said, the Bill contains some very welcome measures. Although the detail will be worked through in Committee, I think we can be positive about the reforms to credit unions. I made some changes to expand the common bond, and I wish the Government well with their extension of it. I ask the Economic Secretary to examine the issue of the interaction of credit unions and Help to Save. For many of the people who use credit unions, the opportunity, on an automated basis, to sign up to Help to Save—it gives everyone on universal credit the opportunity to save up to £600 a year, and after two years receive a 50% bonus from the Government—in these times would be very welcome. I am not sure exactly how that would be achieved, and I realise it is complicated, but it just stands to reason that it should be more readily accessible. I also welcome the reform of consumer credit. These matters were discussed in my office four or five years ago, and I welcome the Government bringing it forward. I certainly did not seek to slow it down, but it is an incredibly complicated piece of work to update our consumer credit framework and how we protect consumers in a world where financial products and the interactions of consumers when taking out products have transformed considerably over the last 52 years. However, as we look at the changes—I note the comments of the Chair of the Treasury Committee, the hon. Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier), on the Financial Ombudsman Service changes—we have got ourselves into a bit of a mess in this country. In the Treasury Committee, I found myself talking about motor finance, and reflecting on being told that harms have been done to me when, from my perspective, I had made a decision about the amount of the deposit and the monthly payment in a financial agreement. However, I fully accept that the consumer credit legislation as it is at the moment means there was an obligation of proactive disclosure on behalf of whoever provided me with that product, rather than some reasonable test of what I should reasonably ask of the person providing the product. To me, that goes to the heart of the dilemma we face in financial services: to what extent can we in this place legislate against risk or put some reasonable responsibility on an individual consumer to take ownership of the decisions they make?
I am very happy to give way to hon. Gentleman, as he did to me.

I am sure the right hon. Gentleman was anticipating my intervention, as we have had this conversation in the Select Committee. I made a point earlier about information asymmetry. Does he not accept that when financial products can be so complex, if providers are not utterly up front about the conditions, it is quite impossible for the consumer to take the responsibility he implies they should take?

I absolutely take on the challenge, but I think we need to level with the British public about this and have a better conversation about it, rather than say there is an ultimate backstop provision apparently for absolutely everything. We have to reset that dynamic. I have mixed feelings about the proposed reforms of the Financial Ombudsman Service. I feel it has become an unreliable pathway to resolution, but I am also concerned that by wrapping it into the FCA, as with the decision to apparently streamline regulations by putting the Payment Systems Regulator into the FCA, we will just create a bigger FCA, with different functions under one banner.

It is worth noting that, in the end, there were two redundancies as a result of the merger, all the backroom costs were the same and the only thing that will change, when the legislation finally goes through, is that the board will go, which is a saving of about £100,000.

I am very grateful for the hon. Lady’s characteristic grasp of the detail of this subject, and she absolutely makes the point. Just removing a banner from a front office does not streamline, so I urge the Economic Secretary to retain a forensic view, as I know she will, of what processes faced by businesses and consumers are actually streamlined. I note the streamlining of the senior managers and certification regime by abolishing mandatory annual employee certification below senior manager level. I note the comment of the hon. Member for Great Yarmouth (Rupert Lowe), who is no longer in his place, on that regime, which was, “Abolish everything.” I understand the frustration that leads to many people saying that, but I think we have some new challenges, which have not been properly addressed, when it comes to AI in financial services. The Chair of the Select Committee mentioned this in passing, but AI, in automating the evaluation of which products would suit individuals, is transforming most consumers’ interactions with financial services. Following the Mills review, there does seem to be a bit of a gap in what will happen with appropriate regulation. It seems that the essence of the position of the FCA is that it does not want to slow down the pace of innovation and growth in financial services, so it will be very reticent to put in any regulation. That is not an unreasonable sentiment, but we must discuss where we as a society feel responsibility should lie. If a financial services firm essentially allows an AI regime to produce offers of products that are sold, somebody has to be responsible for the terms and the basis for such a product going to market. I welcome the changes to the PRA to streamline the bank rules on ringfencing, but I was the Minister who commissioned the Keith Skeoch review, which essentially came to the conclusion that it was not really necessary, but because of the legacy of the global financial crisis, we had better keep it in place. I urge the Economic Secretary to ask this question: what does that ringfencing actually give us? Many senior people at the PRA told me that we do not really need it, and we have a resolution regime that would actually satisfy all our requirements. However, it has a totemic significance, because it is associated with that season of under-regulation that led to the global financial crisis. We must have an honest conversation, not one based on received wisdom about what happened 18 years ago. We should not be reckless, but we do not need to carry unnecessary burdens when they do not really add anything. Time goes quickly in this place, and I respect the need for everyone to speak, but I would like to make two or three broader points. One is about the imbalance of power and expertise. When I became the Economic Secretary, I hardly slept for the first few weeks because it was just so complicated, after I had been the arts, heritage and tourism Minister. From museums to MiFID in one step was a big move, but I did my best to master it. Every six weeks or so, I met the head of the FCA and the head of the PRA. These are some of the most brilliant people in public service, who have at their disposal some of the most intelligent, numerate individuals who are aware of all the nuances of different conditions, the capital requirements of banks of different sizes and the different mitigations for them. I was trying to mediate all the representations I had had from TheCityUK, UK Finance, the Association of British Insurers, the London Market Group and all the consumer organisations, essentially to try to challenge them on the right way of liberalising the regime or having a strong and simple regime to, for example, make it easier for smaller banks. I probably got that right sometimes and on other occasions did not press hard enough, while at times there was a reasonable expectation that I would be moved on. Indeed, since July 2022 there have been eight Economic Secretaries—I am glad the

I thank my right hon. and learned Friend the Minister for her work in bringing the Bill to Parliament, and the other place for its scrutiny to date. I should begin by making it clear that before being elected, I worked in supervision at both the Prudential Regulation Authority and the financial market infrastructure directorate at the Bank of England. I associate myself with some of the comments others have made about the importance of the financial services industry not just to London, but to the whole of the UK. I would like to begin by welcoming the Government’s retention of the proportionality requirements, following debate in the House of Lords. Although I worked on the larger financial companies when I was a frontline supervisor, the proportionality lens was very important in day-to-day decision making, alongside a robust risk framework, not least because as the person who had to deliver a message to a firm, I needed to make sure that I could justify it. In line with that risk-based and proportionate approach to supervision, which I believe is the right one, I wonder if the Bill could make more of the opportunity to stimulate growth in the commercial and specialty insurance markets. The London insurance market is a world leader, with annual income larger than its five closest competitors combined. It insures everything from planes to nuclear power stations, and has an important role to play in helping the Government to tackle climate change, protect against cyber-threats and unlock investment across the UK. As others have said, it competes internationally against markets in places such as New York, Singapore and Hong Kong. Its market is for sophisticated corporate clients, professional investors, insurance firms, banks and pension funds, rather than the individual purchasing travel insurance ahead of a holiday or pet insurance for the family dog, but currently the supervisory approach is rather similar for those very different types of customers. Will the Minister and the Government consider whether more could be done in the Bill to differentiate the way we supervise wholesale insurance markets that have professional clients versus retail markets, where the focus, quite rightly, is on protecting the individual consumer? An obvious example to follow would be Australia, the country of my birth, which makes that distinction between wholesale and retail insurance through the Australian Corporations Act 2001, and tailors its supervision accordingly. There is scope in the Bill to consider what a UK version of that approach could look like to ensure that regulation is proportionate while maintaining strong protections where they are most needed. I support the Government reintroducing the power to be able to act quickly after the access to banking services review reports, but hope that when it is reintroduced it will be narrower in scope to address the concerns raised in the other place that saw the original provision removed from the Bill. It is also important that any action that follows from that review is properly consulted on. In my constituency, my initial efforts to get a banking hub were frustrated by the focus on access to cash under the current rules, when it is really access to face-to-face banking, advice and services that my constituents want to have, particularly on the Strood side of the River Medway and in the more rural populations on the Hoo peninsula. Digital inclusion is very important for people of all ages, but we know that the over-65s in particular place a lot of value on face-to-face banking services and it is important that they do not lose out. Age UK statistics from September suggest that 1.4 million over-65s are fully digitally excluded. Banking hubs can be part of the digital inclusion plan if we follow the example of places such as Singapore, which I know from a recent visit with the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee has very high levels of digital take-up and success using

My hon. Friend is making an excellent point, and I have a similar need in my constituency. Does she agree that the benefits of banking hubs extend to many disabled people, as well as to older residents?

I absolutely agree with my hon. Friend that they should be part of our efforts to ensure that our services are as inclusive as possible. Moving on to the Government’s aim to halve the burden of the senior managers and certification regime for firms, the cost saving is expected to be material. The Bank of England quotes an estimated £2 billion over a decade. It is important that those who present the biggest systemic risk to financial stability remain on the hook if things go wrong. There were very good reasons why the SMCR was introduced after the 2008 global financial crisis and there is scope for streamlining and shorter processes, but we must remember, as we do that, how few people were accountable for the risks that were run in the lead-up to the crisis and how the taxpayer was left to pick up the bill. Once again, it is a question of balance in proportionality and risk. We must always ensure that we maintain high standards of conduct and accountability. Finally, on authorised push payment fraud, I believe that during debates in the other place the Minister said that there were other vehicles, such as the Government’s online safety legislation and fraud strategy, to address APP fraud and so provision was not needed in the Bill. However, we should consider whether the tech giants have been required to sufficiently take on their share of the responsibility for tackling this pervasive harm. The economic cost of APP fraud is significant. It was estimated at £450 million from UK businesses and individuals in 2024, although thankfully the Payment Systems Regulator reports that reductions have been achieved since then, thanks to the APP reimbursement policy. Call me cynical, but I think the only way that online tech giants will care about tackling APP fraud is if they also have some responsibility for reimbursement, rather than it all falling to the retail banks. They should also be held to higher standards for preventative measures, such as user identity verification and enhanced fraud monitoring. To conclude, I welcome the Government’s approach and the progress being made through this legislation, but hope that Ministers will remain open to further refinement. Working in partnership with industry, regulators and Parliament, we have an opportunity to strengthen the UK’s position as a world-leading financial services centre, while maintaining the high standards and consumer protections for which our system is rightly respected.

We on the Liberal Democrat Benches broadly support the Bill. Modernising a framework that has grown complex over decades is sensible and there is much here to welcome, from wider credit union membership to protecting in-person banking and tougher defences against financial crime. I want to use my brief time to talk about a missed opportunity, and I hope the Government will take me up on it. It relates to the Chancellor’s former job. The Government rightly want to rebuild our defence industry, and small firms are one of the bedrocks of that goal. With the way that warfare is accelerating, the cutting, bleeding edge is with small tech firms innovating in things such as AI and autonomy. The Ministry of Defence works with around 12,000 small and medium-sized enterprises through its supply chains, and spends about £5 billion a year with them. It is further set out in the defence investment plan and the strategic defence review that the MOD wants to spend a further £2.5 billion with SMEs by the summer of 2028. That is where defence is moving—if we want to win wars in the modern age, we have to have a robust defence SME sector, Every small business, no matter what sector it is in, knows how hard it can be to raise finance, but many defence firms face an extra barrier. They are often refused bank accounts, loans or insurance simply because they work in the defence sector. SC Group—formerly Supacat—has won MOD contracts worth tens of millions of pounds, yet it has struggled to get investment or loans because it is not seen as acceptable. Another example is 4GD, which uses AI and robotics to run training simulators for British soldiers; the company stopped attending investment meetings and was actually turned away from one once the host found out it was a defence firm. A couple of years ago, 15 SME defence firms formally raised the issue with their trade body, ADS, as they had actually had accounts closed by UK financial institutions. Obviously, those were just the firms that were willing to speak up; there are plenty that will have suffered adverse reactions when seeking credit but have chosen not to speak out—because what firm wants to advertise that they are unable to get capital or credit? The crucial point is that this is not because of regulation. In March 2025, the FCA stated very plainly that: “There is nothing in our rules, including those related to sustainability, that prevents investment or finance for defence companies.” The problem is that many investment and financial services firms have environmental, social and governance policies that explicitly name defence firms as being unacceptable for investment. The Government know that, because in the MOD’s SME action plan, which was published in July, they commit to working with everyone, from venture capital to high street banks, to make it easier for the financial sector to back defence SMEs. But there is a difference between knowing about a problem and setting out a robust way of fixing it, and that is what I want to focus on. The Bill started in the House of Lords, where my noble Friend Baroness Kramer tabled amendment 67, which proposed a practical step that might go some way towards solving the problem. The amendment essentially required the Financial Conduct Authority to review how easily SMEs in sectors critical to our national security can get finance. More specifically, that review would examine the availability and cost of finance for defence firms, whether the FCA’s rules create barriers, whether lenders’ ESG policies, sector exclusions or risk assessments are shutting defence firms out, and whether defence SMEs find it materially harder to get finance than firms in other industries. Crucially, the review would finish with the changes that should be made to improve access to finance for defence SMEs—it should speak to the problems identified in the review. When my noble Friend Baroness Kramer presented the amendment, among a package of others, the Government decline

This is my first speech in this House since being appointed as the Government’s co-operatives and mutuals champion, a role that speaks to my purpose in public life and gives me the responsibility of championing the co-operative and mutuals sector across Parliament and Government. It is a pleasure to contribute to a debate with my right hon. and learned Friend the Economic Secretary sat on the Front Bench; I know she is a champion for the sector in a diverse and resilient financial market. In the spirit of cross-party consensus that we have had this evening, I also pay tribute to the hon. Member for Wyre Forest (Mark Garnier), who I know secretly carries a co-operative dividend card in his wallet and is a champion of the sector as well. I am proud that this Government have an ambitious plan to double the size of the co-operative and mutual economy, and this Bill will contribute to that ambition. I am proud to take on the role that I have been given, because mutuals, building societies and credit unions embody a simple but powerful idea: that financial services should work in the interests of the people who use them. They are owned by their members, rooted in their communities and focused on long-term value rather than simply short-term shareholder returns. On taking the role last week, my first meeting was with the boards and executives of building societies from across the country, and this morning I met with Royal London. I put on record my thanks to the boards of all our building societies and credit unions, and the staff who work for them and support them in their endeavours, providing growth in every postcode already. We see people like this working in our building societies and mutuals across the country. We have seen this movement in Peterborough, just like in many other cities. In 1954, the Co-operative Permanent Building Society opened its office in our city. More than 70 years later, now as Nationwide, it continues to serve and help people to save, buy a home and access trusted financial advice. That long-term commitment to communities is exactly why building societies and the wider mutual movement remain such an important part of our economy and financial services. It brings somewhere to save, somewhere fair to borrow and somewhere that understands the communities that the institutions serve.

I am a director of Slemish ń tha Braid Credit Union. Will the new champion meet me, the Irish League of Credit Unions and the Ulster Federation of Credit Unions to ensure that the support he is talking about covers the whole United Kingdom and all the savers who use those services?

One of the delights of my role will be juggling my diary to meet all the brilliant different mutual movements and community banks and assets across everywhere represented in Parliament—I will be delighted to do so. In particular, I welcome reforms to the credit union common bond. By increasing the membership limit, we can help credit unions to reach more communities, widen access to affordable credit, and help more people to build savings and financial resilience. At a time when many families are still feeling pressure on household budgets, access to fair and affordable lending matters more than ever. Credit unions provide a trusted alternative to high-cost lenders and, as other Members have said, they play an important role in tackling financial exclusion. The Bill also gives us an opportunity to recognise the contribution that building societies make to banking access. Across the country, many banks have reduced their physical presence, yet building societies have continued to invest in local services and maintain branches. Evidence cited by the Building Societies Association shows that building societies now account for around a third of UK banking branches, operating more than 1,400 branches nationwide. That commitment should be recognised and encouraged, but any future banking access requirements must also be fair—building societies cannot be expected to become the catch-all provider for responsibilities abandoned by others. We need a framework that reflects local need, supports innovation and ensures that mutuals are not penalised for continuing to serve the communities that others have left behind. I echo comments made by my hon. Friend the Member for Harrow West (Gareth Thomas) and the Chair of the Treasury Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier), that the rules governing capital and mutuals need to be looked at as well, so that we do not leave the mutual movement behind as we modernise and reflect on financial services as a whole. More broadly, regulation should reflect the distinct nature of mutual organisations. We can maintain strong consumer protections while ensuring that the rules are proportionate and support growth, competition and innovation. Mutuals are not asking for special treatment—they are asking for a level playing field of access and role. The test for this legislation is straightforward: will it help people to save, borrow and own a home? Will it support access to financial services in every community? Will it enable mutuals, building societies and credit unions to grow and serve more people? Mutuals, building societies and credit unions are a vital part of the future of our diverse, resilient and community-focused financial services sector, and I hope the Minister will ensure that the legislation helps them to grow, to serve more people and to continue making a difference in communities such as mine in Peterborough and those of the hon. Members we have heard from this evening.

I want to pick up on the Chancellor’s comments in opening the debate, when he said that he wanted to continue moving the Bill in “the right direction” with a collegiate approach across the House. I intend to table an amendment to the Bill on one specific issue, which builds on the work of Baroness Hoey of Lylehill and the British Insurance Brokers’ Association. It relates to an ongoing campaign of mine to tackle the rising and disproportionate cause of car insurance costs across Northern Ireland. The amendment will seek to include claims management companies in Northern Ireland under the FCA regulations. As it stands, Northern Ireland remains the only part of the United Kingdom where claims management companies are not regulated by the FCA, due to the fact that the Northern Ireland Assembly was not sitting when the legislation was introduced in England, Scotland and Wales. With no room to legislate under the current timetable and an Assembly election coming in May—who knows what happens after May—I believe that the Bill provides the perfect vehicle for bringing forward the solution to what is a technicality on the support of claims management companies and car insurance users in Northern Ireland. Motorists across Northern Ireland continue to face disproportionately high premiums, placing severe financial pressure on our households and particularly on young drivers. Unregulated claims management companies actively pursue customers after collisions and can take anywhere between 15% and 30% of compensation payouts, which significantly inflates overall claims expenses. Those excessive costs then act as a major driver pushing up the cost of car cover for our drivers.

I know that the hon. Member has been working extensively on this matter. He rightly highlights Northern Ireland’s higher premiums; there are also fewer providers, as well as the matter of the unregulated claims management companies. He will know that public transport and cycle infrastructure is failing as well, driving more people into their cars. Does he agree that it is a symptom of Stormont’s failure that another collapse meant that this gap was not plugged, and does he share my concern about the sluggish response of Stormont on providing data and agreeing to co-operate on this matter, and the belief of many drivers that nobody is really at the wheel?

The hon. Lady is correct in some of her assertions on this matter, because correcting this legislative anomaly has not been on the Executive’s agenda. I do not think it will be on their agenda even after the election coming in May. This vehicle—this piece of legislation—does provide the solution for those who need affordable car insurance in Northern Ireland more so than in other parts of the United Kingdom. Extending the FCA’s regulatory remit to Northern Ireland is a vital, practical step to properly govern those firms. It will prevent exploitative practices and bring much-needed fairness to our local insurance market. While various factors contribute to higher insurance costs in Northern Ireland, closing that regulatory gap, which the Bill will be able to do, will actually make a tangible difference. As the Economic Secretary will see, there is support for such a measure across the Northern Ireland parties. It has also been brought in the other House, too. I hope she will listen, and meet me to explore this anomaly and bring about the solution.

It is a pleasure to contribute to this debate and to follow the hon. Member for South Antrim (Robin Swann). Members on all three Front Benches have rightly set out the importance of financial services to the UK economy. It is indeed one of the UK’s most international sectors, and one that holds great significance for the prospects of UK industry, businesses and households across the United Kingdom, including in my constituency. I am very pleased to support the Bill this evening, as it retains the UK’s hybrid combination of strong institutions, high-quality regulators and, ultimately, clear rules that are critical not only to maintaining investor confidence—a currency more valuable than ever before in an incredibly volatile world—to put their money here, but to people and businesses across the UK who use financial services in their everyday lives. Given the limited time I have, I will restrict my comments to a few areas. First, I will mention credit unions and clause 2. My hon. Friends the Members for Feltham and Heston (Seema Malhotra) and for Peterborough (Andrew Pakes), whom I congratulate on his appointment as co-operative and mutuals champion—a very wise choice by the Chancellor and the Economic Secretary—have made incredibly powerful points on credit unions. They are absolutely right to say that the current common bond rules date from another era, when society organised itself very differently. I am pleased that the Bill fixes those matters by ensuring that relatives can join in if they live in different households, that retirees can stay in and join after they stop work, and that students can qualify under the new locality bond. I also welcome raising the membership cap from 3 million to 10 million, as it enables credit unions across the UK to once again have a fair go at expanding and scaling. I want to make a few comments about the regulators. Clauses 15 to 25 reshape how the FCA and the PRA do their jobs, and I welcome the broad direction of travel that the Government have set. Clause 16 makes regulators more considerately and thoughtfully weigh the experience of small and medium-sized firms by having greater regard for proportionality, which is important both in terms of the size of firms that are required to comply with rules and regulations and the cost and benefit of any rule that is made. Having worked supporting smaller quoted companies and then large institutions at the London Stock Exchange Group before I entered this place, it is to me pretty much intuitive common sense that a small firm cannot staff a compliance department or answer every consultation that is issued by Government or a regulator with the same vigour as larger counterparts. It is therefore incumbent on all our regulators—in this case the FCA and PRA, but I would similarly make the comment with regard to regulators operating across our economy—to properly and proactively account for this if they want to be a genuinely constructive partner in supporting economic growth and cultivating meaningfully competitive domestic markets. I also understand that the Government will retain the Lords amendment to keep proportionality as an explicit test in the day-to-day work of both regulators. If that is the case, I very much welcome that. Under clause 19, the FCA and the PRA will be required to report at least once a year on how they are advancing the competitiveness and growth secondary objectives. These reports will feed in the Treasury’s twice-yearly performance reviews with the regulators’ respective chief executives. I think that is a highly appropriate measure, given that almost all the financial institutions—be they large or small, market infrastructure, bank or insurer—were incredibly keen for the previous Government to ensure that regulators adopted such an objective. Given that it has probably been four or five years now since that obligation was placed on our regulators, it is right that those regulators who have such a large impact on our econom

This is quite a wide-ranging Bill, as we can tell from the variety of speeches that we have heard. It focuses not only on financial markets and financial services, but on consumer protection. In some ways, those are opposite ends of the spectrum, and we can talk about anything within that spectrum. I will talk about a few measures in the Bill, but first I want to raise a concern that I have raised before, which is that any piece of legislation that originates in the House of Lords does not take oral evidence. It is immensely frustrating that no oral evidence will be taken regarding this Bill, despite the fact that it is immensely technical and we would really benefit from that. I have been on many Bill Committees, so I know that oral evidence sessions are invaluable for providing information that we can take forward. I urge the Government to have a rethink about whether oral evidence can be taken on House of Lords Bills when they come to the Commons, because it is not fair that we miss out on that evidence. Turning to specific measures in the Bill, part 1 on credit unions is really important, and I agree with widening the membership. I think that the “Fair Banking for All” movement is really positive, and I would be keen to support it, including with access to credit. A number of Members have said things like, “We all rely on banking services”, but some people do not, because they cannot access those banking services because they are so financially excluded. Ensuring that those people who have suffered from economic abuse, for example, have access to those services is really important. I am glad that credit unions will have their common bond widened, but I do wonder about the timeline for the statutory instrument that is coming through to widen the limit of people from 3 million to 10 million. It would be really helpful if the Minister could let us know what is happening with that statutory instrument and when it will progress, because it is happening in parallel to this Bill rather than being included in it. On complaints and consumer redress, I agree with the majority of what the Chair of the Treasury Committee said. I have concerns about the absolute limit of 10 years. I do not think that that is appropriate, and consumer organisations also believe that. I also have concerns about the general principle that consumers should take responsibility for their decisions. As a general principle, that makes sense, but when it comes to specific issues it does not necessarily always work.
