Consumers can take responsibility in situations where they had the full information and the capacity to understand the information that they were given, but in some cases they will not have been given the full information or had the ability to understand it. They should be able to take responsibility for informed decisions but not have to take responsibility for those in which they were not properly informed. I would appreciate it if the Minister could clarify that before we come to Report stage—it relates to clause 7, which proposes amendments to section 228 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. On payment systems regulation, I absolutely agree that changes that can be made. I feel strongly that it is really important to future-proof the regulation of cryptoassets particularly and the transfer of those cryptoassets in relation to payment systems regulation and fees that are regulated by the FCA. Charities have seen a massive increase from a significant number of banking institutions in the payments that they make. For example, charities that have only a small amount of money and might be taking out a float to run a small event will now be seeing massive fees that they were not seeing before because of changes to charitable banking systems. I am not sure whether that exactly falls within payment systems regulation, but I do not think it is fair that they have to do that. Those changes disproportionately harm smaller charities and those who
Order. I call Gareth Thomas, after whom the speaking limit will drop down to six minutes.

I welcome the Bill and commend both the Chancellor and, in particular, my hon. Friend the Economic Secretary for their commitment to modernising financial services. Like the hon. Member for Aberdeen North (Kirsty Blackman) and other Government Members, I welcome in particular the proposed changes to credit union rules as well as recently announced measures to increase funding for community development finance institutions through the British Business Bank. But I want to focus my remarks specifically on what more the Bill could do to ensure that our financial system works for everyone, particularly by improving access to affordable credit for people and businesses in every region. The Prime Minister has rightly said that ours must be a “cost of living Government” putting money back into people’s pockets and giving families breathing space. That must surely include tackling the extra costs that people face simply because they are on a low income. Research published this summer by Fair By Design found that 95% of low-income households pay a poverty premium, of an average of £380 a year extra, for essentials such as energy, insurance, food and, crucially, credit. That research suggests that some 98% of households in poverty in my constituency pay a poverty premium that includes £178 a year on credit. That is not by any definition a small amount for a family already struggling to make ends meet. A household with savings can, for example, replace a broken fridge outright, but almost 40% of UK adults have less than £1,000 in savings and one in four people in financially vulnerable circumstances have no savings at all. A household without savings in that situation might have to borrow at eye-watering rates, paying far more for exactly the same appliance. The people with the least paying the highest price during a cost of living crisis is particularly unjust, and sometimes the consequences are far more serious than higher interest payments. The Centre for Social Justice estimated earlier this year that close to 2 million people in England are borrowing from illegal money lenders. These loan sharks can trap people in escalating debts, using intimidation, threats and sometimes violence to extract repayments. The number of people using them has risen and sadly will continue to rise unless people have safe, affordable alternatives. Credit unions and community development finance institutions already provide those alternatives, but they need support to be able to scale up and meet demand. Public funding, while important and welcome, cannot do the job alone. Some 850,000 SMEs already view access to finance as a major obstacle to growth, fewer than half of SME loan applications to traditional banks are successful, and in surveys, 40% of SMEs cite the high cost of the loans on offer as a problem for their business. Women business leaders, businesses led by disabled people, ethnic minority business leaders and businesses in the poorest areas of our country all face higher barriers to accessing the finance they need to unlock their expansion plans. Concern has grown that a number of high-cost lenders are exploiting this situation, targeting small businesses with slick, online marketing offering very rapid access to cash. As with the payday lending scandal of a decade ago, these lenders do not have to display or explain the total cost of borrowing or accurate representative rates. The often quite aggressive use of personal guarantees, loan stacking and the behaviour of some brokers are also significant concerns. Court judgments, ombudsman complaints and wider efforts to refinance these loans all underline the need for tighter regulation of the rules on high-cost credit and for bolder measures to improve access to affordable credit. Research for the Treasury and the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade published in January this year by the National Institute of Economic and Social Research underlined how much our increasingly cen

Is the hon. Gentleman aware that a lot of this data is collected already, and that it would not place a significant additional regulatory burden on banks to have to gather it? It is just not being published.

Indeed, the FCA said something similar to me at a roundtable with some charities. What is clearly needed is the will to publish that data and to sort out the remaining gaps in the data. The banks’ success has come through being particularly selective in who they lend and offer detailed financial advice to. Their contributions to helping build the capacity of those financial institutions that do lend to everybody have been much more limited—in some cases, non-existent. It is the responsibility of Government to lead on tackling market failures, but as in other countries, banks in the UK have a responsibility to help, and not enough of them are helping to build the capacity of community banks, credit unions and CDFIs to do so. Just as it was right to ask banks to pay a bit more tax to support people with their energy bills, so we should ask them to work with us to create a more diverse, resilient and, crucially, inclusive financial system that will serve every community in the decades ahead. Everyone in this House surely supports easing the cost of living and delivering good growth in every postcode. Fair access to credit is critical to both those ambitions. I hope that Ministers can be persuaded to back further steps on affordable credit as the Bill progresses. A financial system that works for everyone is fundamental to tackling the cost of living crisis.

I am proud of our world-leading financial services sector and the many constituents I represent who work in it. I put on record my thanks to the Chancellor for announcing measures in the Budget that will continue to help Britain attract global talent to work in those services. Our reputation for strong financial services that respect the rule of law depends on our ability to keep dirty money out of the City and out of our country. The Bill will make huge strides on that through clause 13, on which I will focus. No one should turn a blind eye to the source of funds for an investment, whether into a company, a property, art or even some of our national institutions. The former Foreign Secretary, my right hon. Friend the Member for Tottenham (Mr Lammy), was right to say that this Government’s ambition should be to change our reputation from the dirty money capital of the world to “the anti-corruption capital of the world”. One of the historical weaknesses has been the regulation of legal, accountancy and company service providers, which are sometimes referred to as enablers or potential enablers of money laundering. It should not be a badge of honour that dirty money in our country has spawned an entire genre of excellent books: “Kleptopia”, “Treasure Islands”, “Butler to the World”, “London Falling”—hon. Members can read my review in “The House” magazine—and many more. In my Kensington and Bayswater constituency, we similarly do not celebrate the fact that we are home to numerous sanctioned luxury properties and thousands more whose ownership is unknown or opaque. I invite the Minister to join my next “Kensington Against Dirty Money” walking tour, which will show her the impact of dirty money entering our country—often through the vehicles of anonymous trusts registered in the British Virgin Islands and other overseas territories and Crown dependencies. That distorts our property market, hollows out our local communities and, in the worst cases, leaves properties frozen in limbo. That is not sustainable investment. It does not promote economic growth or shine a good light on our professional services. I am therefore delighted that the Bill will significantly strengthen anti-money laundering measures. The Financial Conduct Authority will take on an expanded supervising role, rather than the more than 20 different professional bodies that currently oversee lawyers’ and accountants’ compliance with money laundering rules. The capacity of those bodies simply does not align with the complexity of modern anti-money laundering efforts, and the incentive for private professional bodies to compete for membership does not align with the most rigorous oversight. For a long time, anti-corruption campaigners have called for this consolidation. I pay tribute to those organisations. As the Bill progresses, the transition will need to be managed. There is a clear risk that, as responsibilities shift to the FCA in cohorts, some firms will be left behind. It would be helpful for the Government to provide a reform road map that makes it clear that existing anti-money laundering duties will apply. Funding is obviously key—other Members will speak to the benefits of an economic crime-fighting fund, which the Minister already knows my views on well—but enforcement also means ensuring that the FCA has the right powers to inspect legally privileged material when that is necessary for anti-money laundering supervision. The Minister will no doubt be aware of the action taken by Carter-Ruck against the Solicitors Regulation Authority to challenge its statutory power to compel disclosure, which the SRA has now appealed to the Supreme Court. There is a risk that the FCA will therefore inherit a legally flawed responsibility for anti-money laundering. It is crucial to get that right, and I hope this Bill is the place to do it. On property investment, I know that the Government are committed to looking at the issue of abuse of trust, and the anti-corruption c

I have spoken before about the issue of hidden credit liabilities and the role of the Financial Conduct Authority, and the Bill touches on some of the concerns I have raised. My constituents James and Becky Glanville built a successful family-run nursing home business, but it was destroyed by undisclosed risks embedded in complex financial products sold by NatWest, part of RBS. They were never told that interest rate swaps carried significant liabilities that would be treated as secured debt, erode their borrowing capacity and trigger covenant breaches as interest rates fell. Despite clear regulatory requirements for transparency and informed consent, those risks were never disclosed. The regulatory framework then let my constituents down, too. The FSA and FCA’s redress scheme excluded the hidden credit lines from its review, denying fair compensation to victims like the Glanvilles. The regulator effectively colluded with the banks to suppress this fraud and reduce compensation costs, and by 2019 the Glanvilles were owed £6.3 million, but to date they have received absolutely nothing. The Glanvilles’ case is not isolated. It reflects a wider systemic failure and underscores the urgent need for a full independent investigation and a fair, comprehensive redress scheme. I would be interested to hear the Economic Secretary’s views on the issue and whether the Bill would have protected the Glanvilles had it been in place at the time. After a decade and a half of austerity, an estimated 4.4 million people have taken out £13 billion-worth of credit to pay for essentials. According to the Centre for Responsible Credit, over a million households have potentially been lent to irresponsibly in the last two and a half years. We know that when the rules are vague, it is borrowers who ultimately pay the price. When the cost of living crisis has already pushed household budgets to breaking point, the Government must not undermine the vital safety net that underpins consumer trust in the entire financial system. The FOS is a vital safety net for consumers when something goes wrong, but clause 7 introduces a vastly more complex system for how the FOS determines complaints. The shift from a level playing field with an impartial fairness test to one that initially presumes the firm was in the right means that consumers could now face a harder uphill battle to receive redress and could even be denied the redress they would have received under the old test. The Bill’s stated aim is to introduce deregulation to stimulate growth, but there are serious questions to be asked. Who determines the rights of consumers? Who determines the obligations of firms? Who determines the balance between commercial freedom and public protection, and ultimately, who answers when that balance proves inadequate? We know that the more authority Parliament delegates to the FCA, the more essential it becomes to preserve democratic accountability. That matters when the rights of ordinary citizens are at stake, and particularly when there is good reason to question the FCA’s judgment and priorities. We cannot simply place all the responsibility on to borrowers. I hope that the Economic Secretary to the Treasury will be able to provide some much-needed reassurance on these genuine concerns.

Having worked for more years than I like to remember in financial services, I recognise the importance of regulation, but I also recognise that at times, regulation can be restrictive to economic growth, and given the size and contribution of the financial and insurance services industry, it is rightly an area of focus for reforms. Consumer protection is vital, but I am pleased that the Bill looks to simplify regulation while maintaining high protections and regulatory standards. I want to focus on two areas of particular interest to me. The first is the abolition of the Payment Systems Regulator and the transfer of responsibilities to the FCA. When I chaired the all-party parliamentary group on open finance and payments—the hon. Member for Carshalton and Wallington (Bobby Dean) has now taken over—this was a matter of regular discussion and interest for many members. Currently, four bodies are responsible for regulating different parts of the payments system: the Bank of England, the Payment Systems Regulator, the FCA and the PRA. Absorbing the PSR’s responsibilities into the FCA is a sensible reform, and it sits alongside the Government’s plans set out in the “National Payments Vision” in 2024. The payments sector has spent untold resources trying to satisfy two distinct bureaucratic masters on identical operational metrics, submitting duplicate data on financial crime and systemic resilience. By integrating those systems under a single FCA handbook framework, we can strip out this waste and allow our scaling payments and open banking firms to reinvest that capital back into technical development and national and international growth. The core message from the industry is that the absorption of the Payment Systems Regulator must be strictly managed to protect the open banking and payments sector from transitional friction, accelerate open banking rails and ensure that a single regulatory structure does not slow down the competitive dynamism of the UK’s payments sector. The Payments Association has warned that without precise detail of the merger, it risks being a “reshuffle” rather than a reform, and we must avoid that. Another area of particular interest to me is the plan to widen access to credit unions through the expansion of their common bond in clause 2. When I was chair of the all-party parliamentary group on fair banking, I was often lobbied by organisations such as Fair4All Finance, which made passionate calls for the expansion of credit unions and CDFIs. In 2025, there were around 1.53 million credit union members in Great Britain, but that is equivalent to only 2% of our population, compared with around 40% in Northern Ireland and 64% in the Republic of Ireland. Credit unions are much closer to their communities and their members, and therefore much better set up to take objective, local lending decisions, made by a human, based on the circumstances laid out in front of them, as opposed to a “computer says no” approach.

My hon. Friend is making a really important argument about the financial inclusion reforms. Does he agree that equally important is the Minister’s commitment to finally tackle in this Bill the age-old problem that the parents of disabled children are unable to access their child trust funds by bringing forward reforms that will take away the bureaucratic Court of Protection process?

My hon. Friend must have been reading my speech, because I am about to talk about financial inclusion, and I agree with her. Having worked in banking when child trust funds came out, I know that they were a fantastic initiative by the former Labour Government, but we now need to close the gap to ensure that those adults—they are no longer children—can get access to the funds, whoever they are. In the drive for greater financial inclusion, the credit union model can be incredibly effective, so increasing the common bond limit from 3 million members to 10 million members is a positive move forward. While that measure is not in the Bill, I am pleased to hear that it will be implemented via secondary legislation. Relaxing common bond rules on who can be a member—for example, to relatives of an existing member, people who live in the same household as a member, retirees from a firm in the local area, and students who study but do not live in the area—is an excellent feature of the Bill. Those moves are all welcomed by the Association of British Credit Unions Ltd, Fair4All Finance and the Building Societies Association. Credit unions are invaluable assets in ensuring that people are not financially excluded when they need support the most. An unexpected expense does not disappear because someone cannot access mainstream credit. Expanding access to safe and affordable alternatives to high-cost and illegal lending should remain an important part of the Government’s wider financial inclusion agenda. We should also recognise the key role that credit unions play in encouraging members to save on a regular basis. I want to see more credit unions opening and expanding across the country. For example, in my constituency, we have access to only one credit union, which is in north London. However, if I search by my childhood home in Liverpool, I see that I would have had access to five different credit unions. In fact, Fair4All Finance carried out research involving 1,000 members across those five credit unions and found that they offered increased access to essential affordable credit, supporting people’s financial resilience. Nearly half of the members’ most recent loans were below £1,000—a market that is not typically served by mainstream lenders, but vital for households managing small ups and downs. The credit unions encouraged the development of saving habits, with nine in 10 members reporting that they saved regularly, and half of the members making regular deposits of £20 or more—that is not much, but it is better than nothing—including those on low incomes. Around eight in 10 respondents reported a positive impact on their wellbeing, mental and physical health and family life as a result of their membership.

My hon. Friend is making a powerful point, and he is right to identify credit unions as a brilliant opportunity. In America, some 145 million people use credit unions, compared with a very small amount of the British population. How can we catch up with our transatlantic cousins?

I agree with my hon. Friend; I was just about to conclude by saying that the continued growth of credit unions and the CDFI market is essential. I encourage the Minister and her team to continue to remain open to further options for expanding reach, including to SMEs, so that we can truly drive forward good growth in every postcode.

As a former banking employee, let me be clear that a strong financial regulatory system and strong economic growth are not competing objectives. If Britain is to remain one of the world’s leading financial centres, we must ensure that it is not also one of the world’s preferred destinations for dirty money. As the chair of the APPG on anti-corruption and responsible tax, I have consistently worked with colleagues, including my hon. Friend the Member for Kensington and Bayswater (Joe Powell), to strengthen the UK’s response to economic crime. After a number of meetings with the Economic Secretary to the Treasury and her predecessors, I am pleased to see that she has taken up the cudgel of anti-money laundering supervisory consolidation—that is a bit of a mouthful. That matters, because those who wish to subvert our financial and professional services sectors, launder their ill-gotten gains and drag down the UK’s reputation as a clean place to do business will always seek to exploit the weakest point in our regulatory and supervisory armour. To that end, I am proud to support the Bill, which will modernise the way in which the legal and accountancy sectors, and trust and company services providers, are supervised for money laundering risk, with those responsibilities consolidated within the Financial Conduct Authority. Working in the industry, it always baffled me that anti-money laundering oversight is currently divided among 22 professional body supervisors, many of which are also membership organisations. That creates an inherent conflict of interest—it leads to inconsistent supervision, variable enforcement, fragmented intelligence sharing and uneven suspicious activity reporting. The Office for Professional Body Anti-Money Laundering Supervision’s March 2026 progress report perfectly sums up the situation, stating that professional body supervisors “still report common breaches…and no or inadequate firm-wide risk assessment by their supervised population.” The FCA itself is not immune to this; it only took seven formal actions in the period 2024-25, down from a pre-pandemic high of 60 in 2018-19. The total number of on-site visits conducted by all 22 professional body supervisors has not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels. Economic crime is not victimless—it fuels corruption, organised crime, fraud and kleptocracy. It distorts markets, undermines competition and damages Britain’s international reputation. That is why clause 13, which deals with supervisory consolidation, is so important. By ending the fragmented system of 22 separate professional body supervisors and moving towards a single supervisory model for those sectors under the remit of the FCA, this Government are taking a significant step forward. There are three important opportunities to further enhance the Bill that I would be grateful if the Economic Secretary to the Treasury would consider. First, we need a sustainable solution to the chronic underfunding of economic crime enforcement. The anti-corruption APPG has long called for the creation of an economic crime fighting fund. The principle is straightforward: a proportion of receipts from economic crime enforcement, including confiscated assets, penalties and deferred prosecution agreement receipts, should be reinvested into the very agencies responsible for tackling those crimes. Rather than allowing enforcement proceeds simply to disappear into the consolidated fund, we should create a virtuous circle in which successful enforcement generates additional capability for future enforcement. The Government’s 2025 anti-corruption strategy promised to explore the funding landscape for strengthening economic crime enforcement, and I think something could be done within the framework of this Bill. The FCA has secured more than £1 billion in regulatory and criminal fines over the past decade, yet enforcement receipts are largely either returned to the industry through rebates or transferred to the Treasury. I welcome the Bill, and the opportunity to follow so many excellent contributions this evening, particularly those of the Chair of the Treasury Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier), and other colleagues from the Treasury Committee. One of the key items on our agenda in the Treasury Committee over the past year or so has been the Government’s financial inclusion strategy. We made an important recommendation for Ministers to consider whether the Bill should include further targeted powers to intervene if voluntary action fails to secure reasonable access to essential financial services. I am glad that the Government is doing that; the measures in the Bill will give them more powers to protect access to banking services. So many Members have said this tonight, but I suspect we all have constituents who have seen their access to banking services dramatically reduce in recent years. It is right that the Government are giving themselves powers to address that. We want our financial services industry to contribute as much as it can to economic growth, and I endorse the changes to the operation of the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority, both of which are regular attenders at our Select Committee and play important roles in our economy. It seems eminently sensible that both should produce long-term strategies that balance their responsibilities as regulators with the Government’s growth objectives, and I know that many across the sector will welcome efforts to streamline their reporting requirements. My children were of the generation who received child trust fund contributions under the last Labour Government. We promised to create that programme in our 2001 manifesto, and we set it up in 2002. It has assisted many young people with getting started in life. Many invested in ISAs to build up a fund to bring home ownership closer, or funded driving lessons or a first vehicle. It was a tremendous shame that the Government post 2010 scrapped that programme. Inclusion regarding how those child trust funds are managed is critical, and the Bill takes steps to facilitate access to those funds for parents and carers who manage them in situations where the young people concerned are unable to do so themselves. That is long overdue and I, like many others present, have received correspondence from constituents about the issue. I welcome the change.

It will come as no surprise that I also welcome what my hon. Friend is talking about. Does he share my relief that hundreds of his constituents will finally get access to their £2,600—as will mine in Hyndburn—just the same as those young adults who do not have that problem of lacking capacity?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. The funds should be accessible to those young people, and hitherto they have not been. When the money is available, it can help that young person with a start in life and give them the financial means to better themselves at a crucial time. That is a critical measure in the Bill. Credit unions are also critical to inclusion and to this Bill. The legislation contains some important reforms to help us modernise the sector. I was pleased to visit Wave Community Bank over the summer. Along with Greenwich and Bexley Credit Union, it plays a vital role in supporting residents in Dartford to access affordable credit in times of acute financial stress. Awareness of credit unions remains far too low, and these changes are welcome to ensure that more Dartford residents can join them. We know that 37,000 people across my constituency—almost half the adult population—are in financially vulnerable circumstances. Many people have limited savings and a life event, such as a job loss or a break-up, will leave them in a particularly dire situation. That is where credit unions, as we know, can play a vital role. Earlier this year, the Government published the outcome of their call for evidence on reform of the common bond, which included proposals welcomed by the Association of British Credit Unions and Fair4All Finance to widen access to membership. Some of the measures announced in the Bill, including steps to allow students studying locally to join or those retired to maintain their access, are incredibly welcome. I understand that the measures to increase the potential membership cap of the common bond will come a bit later through secondary legislation, but I welcome indications from the Government that the cap is likely to be raised to cover a population of as much as 10 million, from the current 3 million. Taken alongside the very welcome credit union transformation fund, which is there to build operational resilience in the sector, I hope the measures will see a long-term, sizeable increase in membership of credit unions across the country and particularly in my constituency, and see the Government deliver an important part of their financial inclusion strategy. Finally, I join others in expressing concern that the changes to the operation of the Financial Ombudsman Service in clause 6—and in particular the need to refer significant volumes of cases to the FCA—will “gum up the system”, in the words of senior figures in that organisation. This means that consumers may wait longer for less favourable outcomes, which is surely something that Members should not welcome. I am also concerned, alongside others, about the changes to, or indeed the weakening of, the fair and reasonable test in clause 7, as applied to future complaints. Again, this may well reduce the rights of consumers through the process. I hope that when the Minister responds, she will deal with the points made by myself and others about concerns that are clearly important to us all in an otherwise hugely welcome Bill.

I declare an interest as the chair of the all-party parliamentary group on investment fraud and fairer financial services. It was admirably chaired by the hon. Member for Harrow East (Bob Blackman) for a number of years, and I took over 18 months ago. The all-party group grew organically: a number of Members were coming to Parliament with concerns about individual instances of fraud, and as a result, people came together and set up the all-party group. We work on the principle that we all support the idea that we need an effective and vibrant finance sector, but that the foundation of that sector is trust. “My word is my bond”—that is exactly what the whole element of trust is about. There is a real concern at the moment that there is a lack of trust. If we look at the FCA’s polling, 36% of people said they did not feel that they had been treated fairly or honestly by a financial firm, and I can understand why. Let me run through just a few examples from my experience here: payment protection insurance; endowment mortgages; pension transfer mis-selling; London Capital, which I believe my hon. Friend the Member for Bishop Auckland (Dr Rushworth) mentioned; Connaught; Woodford; and hidden credit lines. I warn the House that the issue of micro-bonds is coming down the track as well, and that will be enormous. We can see why people have lost confidence to a certain extent and why, as the hon. Member for Carshalton and Wallington (Bobby Dean) mentioned, we should listen to the 16 organisations that represent consumers, which have come to explain to us their concerns about the Bill. Concerns have also been set out by my hon. Friend the Member for Dartford (Jim Dickson). On clause 7, the concern is the interference with the fair and reasonable test. Way back in the year 2000, when that Financial Services and Markets Bill was going through the House, there was a long discussion that came to a fair proposal to establish the fair and reasonable test in the legislation. If I remember rightly, it was agreed on a cross-party basis. To now introduce conditionality, in terms of compliance with FCA rules, does not necessarily result in a fair outcome; certainly, in many instances, we have found that compliance with FCA rules is just not good enough to secure justice for people. To reassure us, the Chancellor of the Exchequer said, “Don’t worry—the consumer duty will still apply.” It is not in the Bill, as far as I can see. I think that is a real issue. If we are to reassure people out there, we need to ensure that elements of that reassurance are in the legislation. As my hon. Friend the Member for Dartford also said, on clause 6, the issue of having to refer ambiguities from the FOS to the FCA draws the FCA into an adjudication role. I have to say that a number of the cases that we have dealt with have concerned omissions and failures on the part of the FCA. Again, there is an element of conflict of interests there. I know that an element of discretion can be involved, but it is a question of the elements of discretion to which the FCA is subject. The Bill states that the ombudsman must take into account significant implications in relation to the functioning of relevant markets”. I think that the FCA will be under pressure to ignore some of those elements if they fly in the face of issues relating to market success. Clauses 42 and 43 undermine the ringfence between investment and retail banking. I was here in 2008. Others claim it, but it was I who first raised the subject of Northern Rock in this Chamber. We are seeing the same cycle: there is a financial crisis, regulation is introduced, memories fade, there is pressure to reduce that regulation, and we go into another crisis. That is what was happening from the 1980s onwards. Curiously, there were two books that people reached for when the crisis happened in 2008. One was J. K. Galbraith’s analysis of the 1929 crash. The other, funnily enough, was Marx’s “Capital”, but that is another di

The Bill contains many good things that other Members have spoken to. The Chancellor pitched it as a Bill that will unlock investment for growth. If we want people to invest, we need them to have confidence. My right hon. Friend the Member for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell) and I did not collaborate on our speeches, but, as he pointed out, 36% of people surveyed by the FCA believe that financial firms are not honest. When the Bank of England asked people to sum up the finance industry in a word, the word that the British people picked was “corrupt”. The Financial Services Ombudsman is receiving 216,000 complaints a year, and it is easy to see why: £1 billion is now being lost every year in investment scams. The most notable example is London Capital & Finance, but there are others, including Blackmore Bond, Basset & Gold, Astute Capital and Godwin Capital. The Bill addresses complex issues in which I claim no expertise, but I take a strong interest in them because they are of interest to the people I represent. I want to share the experience of ordinary people who have lost their savings to unregulated investment products. I myself lost a few thousand pounds to a scam. I set up a Facebook group years ago, and the first person who contacted me was a man from Manchester. He had worked as a binman throughout his career, getting up early in the morning, working in all weathers and saving for his pension. He took the lump sum of his pension and invested it in Astute Capital. He lost all of it. I want to talk about what that looks like as a process. It begins with an ordinary person searching to compare high-interest savings accounts with banks. They put their contact details on the internet, and then they get unsolicited calls from people with posh accents offering them investment advice and suggesting that they put their money in an ISA. They have probably heard of ISAs, and they know it is a Government-approved and tax-incentivised way to save. The person will admit to them that they are not FCA-regulated, but they probably have not heard of the FCA and may not know what that means. They may also be told that their capital is at risk, but then that nice person with a posh voice explains to them, “I have to tell you that—it’s the legal bit—but let me explain to you why you’re actually okay. Everything you’re investing is fully asset-backed up to several times its value, and we spread the risk across multiple portfolios.” The individual trusts, they invest and they wait three years. They look forward to getting their money back with the interest they were promised, but when that time comes—this happened to customers of Astute Capital—they get told, “We’re sorry; we can’t pay you. But if you just stick with us for another six months, it’s better than causing someone to whom we’ve lent your money to default.” So they wait another six months. Six months later, their bonds are forcibly converted into shares and they are told, “Don’t worry; soon enough you’ll be able to sell those shares, and your shares are worth more than what you invested”—except they are not, and eventually the company goes into administration. And then what happens? The person loses everything. When they investigate it, they find that a director of Astute Capital was simultaneously a director of the firm to which their money was lent. As a director of both firms, he took away the security on the debt. An ordinary person would expect that, in such a situation, there is some sort of recompense. They would think it is illegal, but it is not. People are told that they are at fault because they should have known that they were investing in an unregulated company. I had a man say to me on the phone, “I can’t look my wife in the eye. I’ve lost everything that we’ve saved over all these years.” What happens to the directors? What happened to Timothy John Smith, who was the director of two companies? According to Companies House, he is now at Axecap Ltd, another unre
I call Noah Law to make the final Back-Bench contribution. Those who contributed earlier should make their way back to the Chamber.

I warmly welcome the Bill and its goal of creating a more transparent financial services sector that can continue to play a key role in creating growth and prosperity for the whole of the UK. I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. Having spent a decade in investment banking and financial advisory work, I have some understanding of both the potential of our financial services and the reforms that they need. The proposed reforms to credit unions are extremely positive. By virtue of being owned by their members, credit unions are uniquely incentivised to put surplus profits into providing better services, rates and returns for their members—something that, as a Co-operative Member, I am delighted to support. I am delighted to support the efforts of my hon. Friend the Member for Peterborough (Andrew Pakes) in this space too. The Bill will make it easier for credit unions to accept new members. It removes unnecessary administrative blocks and provides greater support, allowing more people to join credit unions, which are rooted in their communities and committed to delivering for them. Expanding access to credit unions also means access to more affordable lending, which gives those in the most dire financial circumstances access to credit at reasonable rates, instead of leaving them at the mercy of predatory lenders. Credit unions encourage saving, responsible borrowing, and investment in our communities and local economies. The reforms in this Bill will make accessing them easier than ever. As my hon. Friend the Member for Harrow West (Gareth Thomas) pointed out, we eagerly await the response to the review of fair access to banking and capital markets. More widely, I am glad to see the industry support the aims of this Bill and the support for the better regulatory strategy, accountability, deadlines and the proposed improvements to the senior managers and certification regime. By requiring the FCA and the PRA to report annually on their efforts towards competitiveness and growth, we ensure that the Government, regulators and the industry pull together in one direction for the financial sustainability of our country. Additionally, by improving the way in which regulators make decisions, we can improve the confidence of investors in our financial services. The reduction in the statutory period of authorisations and variations of permission from six to four months, and the period for incomplete applications being reduced from 12 to 10 months, ensures a smoother system for firms and leaves a lot less up in the air. Delays in regulatory decisions can be hugely costly for firms, and can even mean postponing fund launches and major investment decisions, and affect firms’ ability to grow, innovate and compete internationally. A simple regulatory system provides greater clarity for firms, better transparency for the public and the Treasury, and benefits us all. I welcome the Bill’s allowing the Treasury to introduce secondary legislation to amend specified determination periods, once again demonstrating the Government’s willingness to work closely with Britain’s most valuable and prosperous of industries. I am very grateful to the Chancellor for his acknowledgment that we have asked the sector to do its bit to contribute to sound and prudent public finances— I would argue that that prudence, to quote the right hon. Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart), who is no longer in this place, “dwarfs” short-term fiscal interventions—and it directly contributes to sound and prudent finances in an otherwise globally turbulent macroeconomic environment, after the public did their bit to safeguard the sector through its most challenging of times. Consequently, we in this House must also give due care and attention to this incredibly valuable sector. I do believe that the Chancellor has shown that, even when those difficult decisions have to be made, this need not be a zero-sum game. I would like to

It is a great pleasure to close this debate on behalf of the official Opposition, and to follow on from my very good friend, the shadow Economic Secretary—my hon. Friend the Member for Wyre Forest (Mark Garnier)—who has done excellent work both in this Chamber and behind the scenes to engage extensively with the industry. Indeed, I am sure there is not a lunch table in the City of London that has not been graced by my hon. Friend—all, of course, in the service of his great country. I draw the House’s attention to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, particularly my long career in asset management, my active involvement in the industry going back many years, and my current chairmanship of the APPG for blockchain, which is relevant to this Bill. It has been a privilege to be joined by many Members from across the House who clearly have extensive industry experience. I firmly believe, as I have for a long time, that we need more people in Parliament who have worked specifically in this sector, and who understand its importance and its power to help and influence our economy and our communities. I thank all Members from across the House for their contributions to the debate, but I will name a few in particular. The Chairman of the Treasury Committee, the hon. Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier) who is not currently in her place, provided a typically detailed and very thoughtful contribution. She expressed concerns about whether the pendulum is swinging away from consumer protection, as well as outlining her concerns about the reforms to the FOS. I do not agree necessarily with everything she said, but the House is better for the scrutiny that she and her Committee provide. Let me pay tribute to our country’s longest-serving Economic Secretary, my right hon. Friend the Member for Salisbury (John Glen), who moved with grace from museums to MiFID back in the day. He spoke about his mixed views of the FOS. He acknowledged that it is—in his words—an unreliable path to resolution, and helpfully warned us that we need to consider the challenges posed by AI to the financial services sector. I congratulate the hon. Member for Peterborough (Andrew Pakes) on his appointment as the Government’s co-operatives and mutuals champion. I have to say it is an appointment that passed me by, but I very much welcome it. One person who has always been a champion of co-operatives and mutuals is, of course, the hon. Member for Harrow West (Gareth Thomas), who spoke of the high cost and burden of credit, especially for those in poverty. We on the Conservative side of the House want sensible deregulation. We want less bureaucracy in our system. We want lower burdens and more growth. Where the Bill does that, we will welcome it and we will help make it happen. The Chancellor was right in his opening remarks when he said that it is important to recognise the cross-party work that has gone on already with the Bill. He rightly echoed the views of those us on the Conservative Benches when it was said in the other place that the Bill moves us all in the right direction. Having said that—I am loath to depart from the happy and collegiate atmosphere of the debate so far—I am reminded of what Disraeli once said: “No Government can be long secure without a formidable Opposition.” So, if Members will forgive me, I have a job to do tonight. In certain areas, as my hon. Friend the Member for Wyre Forest set out, we believe the Bill does not go far enough. I would like to highlight two areas in particular. First, on digital assets, the United States has legislated for stablecoin. South Korea and even the European Union have their own regimes. Our competitors globally are moving ahead. That matters because stablecoins could revolutionise the way we pay for goods and services. Blockchain technologies could transform the way we interact with companies and the state. The Bill was our chance to set out a more advanced vision and pol

It is a pleasure to close this debate on the Financial Services and Markets Bill. I am grateful to hon. Members from across the House for their contributions, including those on the Conservative Benches who have joined us on a one-line Whip. I am grateful, as has been highlighted, for the spirit of collaboration in the other place, and for the constructive criticism—I think—that has been offered here. I know that Madam Deputy Speaker is being strict in the time limits applied to the wind-ups, so I will do my level best to cover as much as I can and spend most of my time addressing the reform of the regulatory landscape, which is where hon. Members have put most focus. To the extent that I cannot cover things, I will follow up in writing. As was pointed out by the hon. Member for Aberdeen North (Kirsty Blackman), I think the breadth of today’s debate reflects the importance of these reforms and, indeed, the importance of financial services to this country. I will start by going back a step, if I might, because this party came into office with a really clear purpose: to bring stability back to the British economy, give working people greater security and get Britain back on the path to prosperity. At Budget, the Chancellor took the responsible decisions needed to protect the public finances and provide breathing space for firms and families across the country. However, stability and fiscal responsibility are the foundations, not the destination. If we want to see more good jobs, opportunities for our young people and people feeling more secure in their finances, we know that we need a thriving, dynamic economy that delivers for the British people. Few sectors are more important to that task than financial services. From providing SMEs with finance to expand, innovate and hire to helping a family to buy their first home, getting capital to some of our most exciting start-ups and supporting people saving for retirement, financial services provide the ecosystem that underpins our economy and each of our daily lives. In Leeds, Bristol, Bournemouth, Manchester, London, Edinburgh, Belfast and Cardiff, financial services right across the United Kingdom provide the services we rely on every day, supporting more than a million good, highly skilled jobs and the ambitions and the aspirations of the country. As hon. Members have pointed out, we are recognised as a world leader in financial services—something that all of us in this place should be very, very proud of, and something we must protect as a critical strategic asset. Members have also pointed out that global competition for capital is intensifying, and it is therefore vital that we strengthen the sector’s ability to deliver for the country, which is exactly what this Bill does. Members have spoken to the key reforms in this Bill. Let me start with child trust funds, an issue raised by my hon. Friends the Members for Hyndburn (Sarah Smith), for Southend West and Leigh (David Burton-Sampson) and for Dartford (Jim Dickson), where we are righting injustice that has existed for far too long. Child trust funds were a product of the previous Labour Government, and they were based on a simple promise: every single child in this country, no matter their background, would start adult life with a financial asset of their own. However, for far too many families of children with disabilities, that reality has been very different. Parents have been forced to go to court in a lengthy and complex process to access their children’s funds on their behalf. That is why we announced last week that we will use this Bill to make it simpler, easier and fairer for parents and carers to access child trust funds on behalf of young people who lack mental capacity. That means that up to 126,000 young people will be able to more easily access funds currently worth an average of £2,600. This money was always theirs, and with this Bill, it will reach them. Many hon. Members—far too many to mention—have rightly h

May I put on record again my concern that, as we may be facing a significant global crisis as a result of AI debt problems, now is not the time to undermine the protections we brought forward after 2008 and, in particular, the separation between retail and investment banking?

I am grateful to my right hon. Friend for his comments. We are approaching our reforms of the ringfence very carefully. A detailed review has been conducted. We have to ensure that where regulation exists, it is fit for purpose and fit for the circumstances of the modern age. I am more than happy to meet him and talk about the new growth allowance, for example, which will ensure that we can get more capital into the real economy, more homeowners on the ladder and more investment to businesses. The Bill will deliver a stronger economy to deliver opportunity, hope and prosperity in every corner of the country. I commend the Bill to the House. Question put and agreed to. Bill accordingly read a Second time. Stepping Hill hospital sits in my constituency. It is one of the busiest hospitals in the region, with over 91,000 patient admissions each year. It serves Stockport, parts of Greater Manchester and parts of Derbyshire. I have raised the issues faced by the staff and patients there many times in the House and been told repeatedly that the Government are working with Stockport NHS foundation trust and the integrated care board to solve them, but time and again we are let down by the lack of real action. On Friday I visited the hospital with my hon. Friend the Member for Hazel Grove (Lisa Smart), and we met senior teams, clinicians, nurses and operational staff.

On the point about nurses at Stepping Hill hospital, as the hon. Member for Hazel Grove (Lisa Smart) knows, my mother did her nurse training at Stepping Hill back in the 1970s. Since it is my mother’s birthday tomorrow, will the hon. Gentleman join me in wishing my mum a very happy birthday and acknowledging the hard work and commitment of the nurses at Stepping Hill hospital?
Mr Jogee, I am sure we would all like to wish your mother a happy birthday, but we are discussing the future of Stepping Hill hospital.

I absolutely respect that intervention, and I do wish the hon. Gentleman’s mother a happy birthday. If it were possible, we would all do a rendition of “Happy Birthday”, but we will leave that for another time. This was not my first visit to the hospital—I have been there several times, both as an elected representative and as a patient—but it was the angriest and most emotional I have ever been while visiting it. On our visit, I saw staff and patients’ dignity taken away from them, I saw a building completely and utterly unfit for purpose, and I saw a health system that was left to rot, quite literally, over the years of Conservative neglect now being given only plasters by the current Government. I am not exaggerating when I say that the visit was harrowing. To see staff and patients suffer in buildings that leaked, surrounded by walls that were rotting and floors that were sinking, was truly awful. It painted a stark and terrible picture of the way our health service is being treated by decision makers in Whitehall, with £120 million being spent each year just on mitigating the damage being caused by the hospital’s crumbling estate. This is an incredibly expensive sticking plaster that does not solve the underlying problems, but instead makes things worse. A comprehensive repair of Stepping Hill’s estate would cost just over £134 million, and the Government must commit to providing that amount to get the hospital back on its feet. It would save money in the long term and mitigate the huge risks the estate poses.

My hon. Friend is absolutely right: what we saw on our visit was harrowing. He talks about value for money and how over £100 million is going on just maintaining the buildings as they currently stand. That is literally plugging holes in the wall. I am sure he agrees that a better use of the money would be to spend capital on building a new additional site in Stockport town centre. That would free up space on the site that is no longer fit for purpose and would be a much more sensible, value-for-money way to spend the money.

I thank my hon. Friend for bringing that idea forward. Yes, absolutely; I will talk later about how a new site in Stockport could alleviate the stress on Stepping Hill and save the Government a lot of money. Stockport NHS foundation trust is clear that the £134 million would be over and above any Government funding already allocated. The trust simply cannot make the efficiency savings being asked of it when it is firefighting each day. I want to tell the House what this looks like and how this firefighting impacts the day-to-day lives of the staff and the patients they look after. On our visit, nurses told me of the huge issues they face regarding infection control. There are genuine concerns that the outdated and inefficient building makes infection control even harder. Beds are too close to each other and people are unable to move around within a safe distance of each other. Parts of the site predate the NHS and, as such, the corridors are so small that two wheelchairs or trolleys cannot go past each other. Shockingly, the hospital has only around 20% of the side rooms it needs to isolate infectious patients, and in the electrocardiography zone there are no handwashing facilities. The nurses told me that during covid, they had to create massive one-way systems through the wards, making care and movement even more complex. That was a logistical challenge at a time when the NHS was already being tested to breaking point. The building itself is also dangerous. On the visit, I was shown the relentless water damage and leaks across the estate. When it rains, staff race around the hospital putting out buckets to catch the water dripping through the ceiling, sometimes on to vital equipment. Ward and shower rooms have become completely unusable because of leaks, which have further reduced capacity. I have seen wards where sewage comes up through the drains, meaning that nurses have to clean up rather than look after the patients they should be tending to. The glass windows in the cardiology unit are at a huge risk of falling out, posing a serious safety risk. Clay pipework from 1905 is still in use and leaking, meaning that escaping steam is rotting the floors beneath. Some floors are now physically sinking. As I entered the building, I saw that the hospital’s café was closed for that very reason—I could actually see where the floor was beginning to slope down. Scaffolding is literally holding up the glass ceiling in the main entrance— a worrying welcome for patients entering the building.

Many of the hospital’s wards are Nightingale wards, which cannot support contemporary care. As I have already mentioned, these wards do not have enough side rooms. That poses a massive risk in terms of infection control, but it also poses challenges when providing patients with the privacy and dignity they need. When patients are receiving end-of-life care, the hospital cannot always provide a separate room, and instead beds are curtained off to give families the privacy they need. To ensure that people are aware, staff place a candle on the ward entrance to tell others that someone is having their last moments with their friends and family. That was the hardest thing to see on our visit. It makes me so angry and ashamed that families in my constituency are saying goodbye to their loved ones in this way. It is not just the physical infrastructure that needs addressing. Some staff talked me through how outdated computer software and internet connections mean that they have to use memory sticks to take images from one computer to another. Some of the images are for time-critical operations, in which every second counts, yet clinicians, doctors and nurses had no option but to walk memory sticks from one computer to another, wasting precious time. Finally, let me talk about the conditions the staff work in. The ward designs in the older buildings make staffing a serious challenge. Staff-to-patient ratios mean that nurses must look after no more than eight patients, but some wards have 14 beds, meaning that two nurses are required, despite one of those nurses being underutilised. The staff rooms are also completely inadequate; I saw one room that could fit only two people comfortably, despite there being 12 people on that ward, while the staff room on the cardiology unit, which serves 30 people, has only one toilet.

I congratulate the hon. Gentleman, my constituency neighbour, on securing this debate on an important issue for the three MPs who represent the local authority of Stockport. I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests regarding my trade union membership and being chair of the all-party parliamentary group on cancer. All of us in this House would agree that our constituents deserve high-quality, first-class, reliable care in hospitals and from our GPs, and that the staff also deserve high-quality services. I am not sure that I agree with the hon. Gentleman’s suggestion for a new location for a new hospital—I think there should be a wider discussion, but I do not wish to take up too much time in dissecting the Stockport local plan. However, I do agree that Stepping Hill hospital is simply not adequate for patients or staff. Does he agree that in the past two years this Government have allocated £2.5 million for targeted safety works, £26 million for the construction of a new pathology building and £75 million for the Stockport NHS foundation trust over the next four years? That is a stark contrast with the previous 14 years—the coalition Government, of which his party was part, and the Conservative Government that followed.

I respect the hon. Gentleman a lot; we all work well together as Stockport MPs. Although we should never say no to money coming into the hospital, even the NHS trust is saying that this money does not touch the sides, as I have said. We need more investment, and the £134 million repair bill needs to be sorted. We can discuss the need for a different site another time; I am fully behind Stockport needing a new hospital site. I was talking about the staff room for the cardiology unit, which serves 30 people but has only one toilet. That is not to mention the fact that the toilet windows are not frosted over, so there is a massive privacy issue for the staff. I was also told about one member of staff who works in reception in one unit and who uses an electric wheelchair. Horrifyingly, their work environment is completely inadequate, not only because the doors to the unit are not suitable for wheelchairs to go through, but because they cannot access an accessible toilet and so are forced to leave the building in which they work to go to another a few minutes away. Often they have to go out in the rain just to use a facility that they should have the right to use. That is simply a disgrace, and I cannot believe it is happening in 2026. I asked why that person still felt the need to work there even with such basic accessibility requirements not being met. I was told that it was because they cared so much about the hospital, about Stepping Hill and about the job they do that they would not leave. That was a running theme through our visit. Despite all the issues and problems I have laid out, the staff across Stepping Hill maintain excellent standards in conditions that are working against them. They continue to provide an unbelievably caring and wonderful service. They are a credit to the NHS and to Stockport. They never complain or down tools because of the conditions; instead, they get on with the job. My partner Lou and I sadly needed to spend time at Stepping Hill recently. Despite the awful reasons we were there, we felt protected, supported and cared for. I want to take this moment to say thank you to the staff for everything they did for us, for keeping us safe and for looking out for us. I promise here that I will always have their back and will never stop campaigning to get them the hospital they deserve. So what is the solution? The Government announce bits of support every now and then, and they often announce the same pots of money time and again in the hope that it looks like support is there, but that does not help. We need a fully funded strategy for how Stepping Hill will be saved. There were plans for a new hospital in Stockport that were originally rejected by the previous Conservative Government. The plans would have enabled some relief for Stepping Hill and helped free up much-needed space on the estate. The plans also had backing from the trust and the council, which partnered to develop them, and the integrated care board. They pushed as much as they could. Sadly, it does not appear that the hon. Member for Stockport (Navendu Mishra) supported them, but we will talk about that another time. Whatever the solution, the fact is that action is now desperately needed. We cannot go on with more debates, more questions to Ministers and the Prime Minister, more letters to the Department of Health and Social Care and more meetings with officials—the Government have to act now. For over a decade the Conservative Government left Stepping Hill hospital to rot. This Government cannot do the same, and the Minister should not allow that to happen. I want to end with a number of questions for the Minister. First, it is clear what help is needed and required, so why have the Government failed to act so far? Secondly, is it appropriate for 30 NHS staff members to share one toilet and that an NHS worker who uses a wheelchair has to go out in the rain to access the nearest accessible toilet? Thirdly, is it fair that patients at the

I congratulate the hon. Member for Cheadle (Mr Morrison) on securing this very important debate. Throughout it, he and other Members have paid tribute to the work that happens at Stepping Hill hospital, despite what are clearly often very difficult situations, and it is important that that is on the record. Unfortunately, the Minister for Secondary Care, my hon. Friend the Member for Bristol South (Karin Smyth), who is the Minister with responsibility for this, could not be here this evening. I am sorry to be a poor replacement for her, but let me reassure the hon. Member for Cheadle and the House that I will report this discussion to her directly. I know that she is aware of this debate, and I am sure that she will follow up in the appropriate way with the Members concerned. As I said, Members have rightly paid tribute to all the staff at Stepping Hill hospital. The hospital is extremely important to the communities it serves, and its patients and staff deserve facilities that are safe, resilient and fit to deliver high-quality care. I am going to make a few remarks about the overall position with capital investment and how we have got to this point, but none of that is to say anything other than that all patients and staff deserve good-quality facilities. For too long, capital investment in the NHS was insufficient and short term, and the challenges at Stepping Hill reflect a much wider problem across the NHS estate. Capital budgets were repeatedly raided to meet day-to-day pressures, and the result is an estate carrying the consequences of years of under-investment, as has been made clear. There are no quick fixes, but we can change the way the NHS invests in its buildings, moving away from short-term fixes towards sustained investment and proper long-term planning. That is why our 10-year capital plan for health and social care is based on three core principles: more investment; greater certainty, so that investment can be planned over the long term; and greater autonomy for local leaders to decide how capital is best used. First, we are investing more. After years of under-investment, we are providing the largest capital budget in NHS history, with annual spending rising to £15 billion by the end of this spending review period. Within this, the estates safety fund will provide £6.75 billion over the next nine years to tackle the poorest-quality parts of the NHS estate and ensure safe environments for patients and staff. We have already confirmed £1.5 billion of investment in projects through the fund, including £1.3 billion for maintenance, safety and resilience projects across the NHS estate and more than £200 million for major hospital projects. This means that more than 950 schemes are being delivered across the country. That sits alongside around £21 billion in operational capital over this spending review period, empowering local health organisations to invest in their priorities, including their estates. We are also investing around £5 billion over the spending review period to expand and modernise diagnostic, elective, mental health and emergency services, helping to increase capacity, cut waiting times and improve urgent and emergency care performance. Secondly, we are providing greater certainty over that investment. We have provided NHS organisations with multi-year capital allocations to 2030 and a further five years of certainty beyond that for estates maintenance funding to 2035. This stability is designed to provide the confidence needed for long-term investment decisions and responds directly to one of the key NHS capital planning challenges cited by stakeholders. Instead of planning from one year to the next, local NHS leaders can now look ahead, prioritise the most serious risks, plan investment over the longer term and secure better value for the taxpayer. That is particularly important for ageing estates like Stepping Hill, where we need to move away from repeatedly patching up ageing buildings and towa

As my hon. Friend the Member for Cheadle (Mr Morrison) said, any money coming to Stepping Hill hospital is to be welcomed, and the Government should be thanked when they get things right. The briefing we have had from NHS leaders in Stockport says that the total planned maintenance costs over five years are £134 million. That is only basic maintenance—it does not account for any new building projects and does not bring the buildings up to the current standard that we would expect of any new building. I am sure that the Minister agrees that all the money needs to be spent for good value for money. Will she and colleagues in the Department of Health and Social Care agree to look specifically at the project we are talking about for Stockport: a new building? The revenue cost of maintaining that building would be so much lower than continually plugging the holes—literally—with capital spend.

I understand entirely the case that the hon. Lady makes. There will be further opportunities for the region to fund projects at Stepping Hill hospital through its estates safety fund allocation. As I mentioned in response to the hon. Member for Cheadle, I urge the trust to keep working closely and effectively with the ICB and the region, particularly as other funding streams are available. The trust has been allocated another £75 million in operational capital over the next four years. Before I get too close to the end of my remarks, let me respond directly to the other questions asked by the hon. Member for Cheadle. He mentioned issues with toilets, which sound extremely worrying; from the Floor of the House, I urge local leaders to respond. I will make sure that he and Stockport Members receive a written response to those issues and to those related to end-of-life care. Members will understand the importance of end-of-life care and what a priority it is over the coming months and years for us all, so I will look into those issues.

Although Stepping Hill hospital is in the constituency of the hon. Member for Cheadle (Mr Morrison), it serves people from Hazel Grove, Cheadle and Stockport. May I reiterate the invitation from the hon. Member—I would go as far as calling him my good friend, even though we are in different parties—to the Health Secretary and any Ministers in the Department of Health and Social Care to visit Stockport and speak to volunteers, staff and patients there? Will the Minister pass on that message?

I will certainly pass that message on. As the hon. Member for Cheadle mentioned, the current Prime Minister is no stranger to Stockport, so I am sure that I do not even need to let him know what is happening there. We are already seeing some capital investment translate into better facilities for patients at Stepping Hill. The new urgent treatment centre is now open, with five additional consulting rooms increasing capacity, improving patient flow and helping to reduce avoidable pressure on the emergency department. That builds on the hospital’s emergency and urgent care campus, which fully opened in May 2025; that is part of the £639 million of planned capital investment to support NHS performance in the north-west. Given what we have heard this evening, I cannot pretend that what has been done resolves every infrastructure challenge at Stepping Hill—it clearly does not. The pressures facing the hospital have built up over many years and will take time to address, but we are putting the local NHS on a much stronger footing to tackle them. The reforms set out in our capital plan mean that local leaders can look beyond immediate pressures, plan investment over multiple years and target funding towards the areas of greatest need and importance, and that really matters for Stepping Hill. Members from the borough of Stockport have raised very important issues this evening—they are absolutely right to advocate for patients and staff, and I ask them to pass on my thanks to those staff. We do not underestimate the scale of the challenge, but we are delivering vital investment to address the most pressing risks at Stepping Hill while giving local NHS organisations greater certainty and flexibility to plan properly for the hospital’s long-term future. Without doubt, there is much more to do, but this is how we move away from short-term fixes and towards a safer, more resilient Stepping Hill hospital that can continue to serve the people of Stockport for many years to come. Question put and agreed to.
